weeks.assessment_key: Skills quiz: 1) a diary from 1850 — primary 2) an encyclopedia article — secondary 3) an ancient coin — primary 4) a textbook — secondary 5) 3000 BCE to 1000 BCE = 2,000 years 6) 500 BCE to 500 CE ≈ 1,000 years (add the two numbers; strictly 999 since there is no year 0) 7) Nile — Africa; Tigris and Euphrates — Southwest Asia (Iraq); Indus — Pakistan; Huang He — China 8) latitude lines run east–west and measure north/south of the equator; longitude lines run north–south and measure east/west of the Prime Meridian. Timeline: 10,000 BCE to 500 CE with even spacing (e.g., 10 cm per 500 years).

weeks.prep: Gather: photos of stone tools (Smithsonian Human Origins), smooth stones, clay. Bookmark the Smithsonian Human Origins site for tool images and Lascaux/Chauvet virtual tours.
misconceptions: Thinking early humans were unintelligent. Their tools, art and survival skills show sophisticated thinking.
Thinking dinosaurs and early humans lived together. Dinosaurs went extinct about 66 million years before humans.

days.guide: Read about hunter-gatherer life; complete the chart.

questions.q: Why did hunter-gatherers move often?
questions.a: To follow animal herds and find plants as seasons changed.

days.guide: Compare an Oldowan chopper with an Acheulean hand axe.

questions.q: How did tools improve from Oldowan to Acheulean?
questions.a: Oldowan tools were simple flakes and choppers made with a few strikes; Acheulean hand axes were carefully shaped, symmetrical teardrop tools that took planning.

days.guide: The child writes four ways fire changed life.

questions.q: Give four ways controlling fire changed early human life.
questions.a: Cooking food (easier to digest, killed germs), warmth in cold climates, protection from animals, light to extend the day, a social gathering place, hardening tools.

days.guide: View Lascaux and Chauvet images; infer.

questions.q: What do cave paintings suggest about early people?
questions.a: They valued animals they hunted (horses, bison, deer), had artistic skill and possibly beliefs or rituals connected to hunting.

days.guide: The child writes the diary entry.

questions.q: Name two materials hunter-gatherers used for tools.
questions.a: Stone (flint), bone, wood, antler.

weeks.assessment_key: Diary rubric — 4: at least six accurate details (moving with seasons/following herds, gathering plants, hunting with stone tools, fire for warmth/cooking/protection, small bands sharing food, shelters of hides/caves, cave art), first-person voice, no anachronisms; 3: four or five details; 2: few details or anachronisms (farming, metal); 1: inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Gather: world outline map, colored pencils. Print a world outline map.
misconceptions: Thinking people crossed oceans to reach the Americas first. Most evidence points to Beringia and/or a coastal route along it.
Thinking migration was a planned journey. It happened gradually over thousands of years as groups followed food.

days.guide: Map routes with approximate dates.

questions.q: Where did modern humans first live?
questions.a: Africa.

days.guide: Explain Beringia.

questions.q: What was Beringia, and why did it exist?
questions.a: A land bridge between Siberia and Alaska; during the Ice Age much water was locked in glaciers, lowering sea levels and exposing land.

days.guide: Compare Arctic, desert and rainforest adaptations.

questions.q: Name one Arctic adaptation.
questions.a: Fur and hide clothing; snow or hide shelters; hunting seals and caribou.

days.guide: Read about Channel Islands sites (Arlington Springs on Santa Rosa Island, about 13,000 years old).

questions.q: What do Channel Islands sites show about early Californians?
questions.a: People lived on islands off California about 13,000 years ago, so they had boats and used ocean resources.

days.guide: Give the map quiz.

questions.q: How did lower sea levels help people migrate?
questions.a: They exposed land bridges like Beringia that people could walk across.

weeks.assessment_key: Migration map: arrows from East Africa to the Middle East (~70,000–60,000 years ago), to South Asia and Australia (~50,000–65,000 years ago), Europe (~45,000), East Asia, and across Beringia to the Americas (by ~15,000 or more years ago). Quiz short answer (4 = explains adaptation with two environments and specific examples: Arctic — fur clothing, snow/hide shelters, hunting seals; desert — loose clothing, moving between water sources; rainforest — light shelters, gathering fruits, hunting small animals).

weeks.prep: Gather: seeds (beans or wheat berries), cup of soil, images of Catalhoyuk. Soak bean seeds overnight; find an image of Çatalhöyük's reconstruction.
misconceptions: Thinking farming was easier. Farming meant harder work and new diseases, but more food and settled life.
Thinking agriculture began in one place. It began independently in several regions.

days.guide: Map domestication centers.

questions.q: Where were wheat, rice and maize first domesticated?
questions.a: Wheat — the Fertile Crescent (Southwest Asia); rice — China; maize — Mexico (from teosinte).

days.guide: Plant beans; start a log; discuss staying near crops.

questions.q: Why did farmers settle down?
questions.a: Crops needed tending for months, so people stayed near fields to plant, protect and harvest them.

days.guide: List evidence of permanent settlement at Çatalhöyük.

questions.q: Give two pieces of evidence that Çatalhöyük was permanent.
questions.a: Mud-brick houses built side by side (entered through roofs), storage areas, burials under floors, wall paintings — built and rebuilt over centuries.

days.guide: T-chart costs and benefits.

questions.q: Name one cost of farming.
questions.a: Harder labor, diseases from crowding and animals, dependence on a few crops, more inequality.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test.

questions.q: What is a food surplus and why does it matter?
questions.a: Extra food beyond what's needed; it lets some people do other jobs (specialization).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test sample: 1) primary vs. secondary 2) BCE/CE math 3) Oldowan/Acheulean tools 4) uses of fire 5) Beringia 6) wheat — Fertile Crescent (~10,000 years ago); rice — China; maize — Mexico 7) Çatalhöyük — early town in Anatolia (Turkey) 8) a surplus allows specialization. Constructed response: Paragraph rubric — 4: clear topic sentence answering the question, at least two specific accurate pieces of evidence (named source, artifact or fact), explanation linking each to the claim, concluding sentence; 3: accurate but only one piece of evidence explained; 2: general statements without evidence; 1: inaccurate or off-topic. Expected content: farming allowed permanent villages, food surpluses, population growth, specialized jobs and property, but also more work, disease and inequality.

weeks.prep: Gather: baking tray, soil, water, map of Mesopotamia. Prepare a tray with soil for the irrigation model (outside).
misconceptions: Thinking floods were always helpful. Tigris-Euphrates floods were unpredictable and destructive, unlike the Nile's.
Thinking Mesopotamia is a country. It's a region, mostly modern Iraq.

days.guide: Label the Fertile Crescent map.

questions.q: What does 'Mesopotamia' mean?
questions.a: 'Land between the rivers' (the Tigris and Euphrates).

days.guide: Dig a canal in the tray; pour water to test.

questions.q: Why did Sumerians need irrigation?
questions.a: Rainfall was low, so canals carried river water to fields.

days.guide: Read about floods, levees and canals.

questions.q: Why were Tigris-Euphrates floods a problem?
questions.a: They were unpredictable and could be violent, destroying crops and villages.

days.guide: Draw the cause-and-effect chain.

questions.q: How did irrigation lead to cities?
questions.a: Irrigation → more food (surplus) → people could specialize → trade and population grew → cities.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What is silt?
questions.a: Fine, rich soil left by floodwaters.

weeks.assessment_key: Map: Tigris and Euphrates, Persian Gulf, Zagros Mountains, Syrian/Arabian Desert, modern Iraq, Syria, Turkey, Kuwait. Quiz: 1) Mesopotamia means 'land between the rivers' 2) silt from floods made soil fertile 3) irrigation canals brought water to fields 4) levees held back floodwater 5) surplus → specialization → trade → cities.

weeks.prep: Gather: images of the Ziggurat of Ur and Standard of Ur, sugar cubes or blocks. Print images of the Ziggurat of Ur and both sides of the Standard of Ur (British Museum website).
misconceptions: Thinking Sumer was one country. It was a group of independent city-states.
Thinking ziggurats were tombs like pyramids. They were temple platforms.

days.guide: Read about Ur and Uruk.

questions.q: What was a Sumerian city-state?
questions.a: An independent city and the farmland around it, with its own ruler, god and army.

days.guide: Build a stepped ziggurat; discuss its role.

questions.q: What was a ziggurat for?
questions.a: A stepped temple platform honoring the city's patron god; priests and rulers used it to show their power.

days.guide: Analyze both sides of the Standard.

questions.q: What does the larger size of one figure suggest?
questions.a: Greater importance — likely the king.

days.guide: Make the social pyramid.

questions.q: How did religion support rulers' power?
questions.a: Rulers claimed the gods chose them and supported temples, so obeying the ruler seemed like obeying the gods.

days.guide: The child writes the evidence paragraph.

questions.q: Name two cities of Sumer.
questions.a: Ur and Uruk (also Lagash, Kish, Eridu).

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric — 4: clear topic sentence answering the question, at least two specific accurate pieces of evidence (named source, artifact or fact), explanation linking each to the claim, concluding sentence; 3: accurate but only one piece of evidence explained; 2: general statements without evidence; 1: inaccurate or off-topic. Expected evidence: the Standard of Ur's 'Peace' side shows a banquet with the king, the largest figure, at the top and people bringing animals and goods below; the 'War' side shows soldiers, chariots and captives — revealing a hierarchy with kings and nobles at the top, soldiers and workers below, and captives/enslaved people at the bottom.

weeks.prep: Gather: air-dry clay or play dough, chopstick or craft stick, excerpts of the Epic of Gilgamesh (Fordham Sourcebook). Print the Gilgamesh flood excerpt (Fordham Sourcebook); prepare clay.
misconceptions: Thinking cuneiform is an alphabet. It used hundreds of signs for words and syllables.
Thinking writing began for literature. It began for record-keeping (trade and taxes).

days.guide: Show tokens, pictographs and cuneiform; make the chart.

questions.q: Why did writing first develop in Sumer?
questions.a: To keep records of goods, trade and taxes.

days.guide: Press cuneiform into clay with a stick.

questions.q: What was cuneiform written with?
questions.a: A reed stylus pressed into wet clay, making wedge shapes.

days.guide: Read about scribe schools; write the letter.

questions.q: Why were scribes important?
questions.a: Few people could write; scribes kept records for temples, rulers and merchants.

days.guide: Read the Gilgamesh flood episode.

questions.q: What does the flood story suggest about Mesopotamian beliefs?
questions.a: The gods were powerful and unpredictable and could destroy humans; floods were a real fear.

days.guide: Give the quiz and short response.

questions.q: Why did writing matter for government?
questions.a: Rulers could record laws, collect taxes and keep track of resources.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) tokens → pictographs → cuneiform (wedge-shaped marks) 2) written with a reed stylus on wet clay 3) scribes trained for years in schools (edubba, 'tablet house') 4) Gilgamesh was king of Uruk 5) in the flood story Utnapishtim builds a boat after a god warns him. Short response: writing let rulers record laws, taxes and trade, and keep records over time. Tablet: recognizable wedge marks.

weeks.prep: Gather: Code of Hammurabi excerpts (Avalon Project), image of the Hammurabi stele. Print 20 laws from Hammurabi's Code (Avalon Project) and an image of the stele (Louvre).
misconceptions: Thinking 'eye for an eye' applied equally to all. Punishments depended on social class.
Thinking Hammurabi wrote the first laws. Earlier codes existed (e.g., Ur-Nammu); his is the best-known complete one.

days.guide: Read about Sargon and Hammurabi; map their empires.

questions.q: Who created the first empire in Mesopotamia?
questions.a: Sargon of Akkad.

days.guide: Sort 20 laws into categories.

questions.q: Give a category and an example law.
questions.a: Injury: if a man puts out the eye of a free man, his own eye shall be put out (law 196).

days.guide: Compare punishments by class; debate.

questions.q: Was Hammurabi's Code equal for all? Explain.
questions.a: No — punishments were harsher or fines smaller depending on whether the victim was a noble, commoner or enslaved person.

days.guide: Examine the stele image.

questions.q: Why carve laws in public?
questions.a: So everyone knew the rules; it showed the king's power and that laws came from the gods (Shamash is shown giving authority).

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test.

questions.q: What is an empire?
questions.a: Many lands and peoples ruled by one ruler or government.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test sample: Fertile Crescent geography; city-states; ziggurats; cuneiform; Sargon of Akkad created the first empire (~2300s BCE); Hammurabi of Babylon (ruled ~1792–1750 BCE); 282 laws carved on a stele. DBQ short essay — 4: thesis on whether the code was just, uses at least three laws as evidence (e.g., law 196: destroying a free man's eye means losing your own eye; law 198: a commoner's eye — a fine of one mina of silver; law 199: a slave's eye — half the slave's value), considers Babylonian vs. modern standards; 3: two documents; 2: one document; 1: no evidence.

weeks.prep: Gather: map of the Nile, Herodotus 'Egypt is the gift of the Nile' quote, 'Hymn to the Nile' (Fordham Sourcebook). Print the 'Hymn to the Nile' (Fordham) and a Nile map.
misconceptions: Thinking Upper Egypt is in the north. The Nile flows north, so Upper Egypt is south and Lower Egypt is the delta in the north.
Thinking the Nile's floods were destructive like Mesopotamia's. They were regular and predictable.

days.guide: Label the Nile map.

questions.q: Which direction does the Nile flow?
questions.a: North, into the Mediterranean Sea.

days.guide: Read the hymn; list thanks.

questions.q: What did Egyptians thank the Nile for?
questions.a: Water, food and crops, the flood that renewed the fields, and life itself.

days.guide: Make a circular farming calendar; explain the shaduf.

questions.q: What is a shaduf?
questions.a: A lever with a bucket on one end and a weight on the other, used to lift water from the river.

days.guide: Read about Narmer and the double crown.

questions.q: How did the Nile help unify Egypt?
questions.a: It linked communities by travel and trade along one river, making it easier to rule as one kingdom.

days.guide: Make the Venn diagram; quiz.

questions.q: What did Herodotus mean by 'the gift of the Nile'?
questions.a: Without the Nile's water and fertile silt, Egypt would be desert.

weeks.assessment_key: Venn: both rivers deposited silt and supported irrigation and civilization; the Nile flooded predictably and gently and flows north, protected by deserts; the Tigris-Euphrates flooded unpredictably, with fewer natural barriers. Quiz: 1) Herodotus: 'Egypt is the gift of the Nile' 2) delta in the north 3) cataracts = rapids 4) Upper Egypt south, Lower Egypt north 5) deserts protected Egypt 6) Narmer (Menes) united Upper and Lower Egypt around 3100 BCE.

weeks.prep: Gather: apple slices, salt and baking soda, images of Giza and tomb paintings. Prepare a 1:1 salt and baking-soda mix; weigh apple slices.
misconceptions: Thinking slaves built the pyramids. Evidence (workers' villages, tombs) shows paid laborers and skilled workers, plus seasonal farmers.
Thinking mummification was only for pharaohs. Wealthier Egyptians were mummified too.

days.guide: Read about the god-king; draw the pyramid.

questions.q: Why did Egyptians obey the pharaoh?
questions.a: They believed he was a god on earth who kept order (ma'at).

days.guide: Bury one slice in salt/baking soda and leave a control.

questions.q: Why does salt preserve the apple?
questions.a: It draws water out; without moisture, decay slows.

days.guide: Read the Weighing of the Heart.

questions.q: What happens in the Weighing of the Heart?
questions.a: The dead person's heart is weighed against the feather of Ma'at (truth); a light heart means a good life and entry to the afterlife.

days.guide: Research the Great Pyramid using two sources.

questions.q: Who built the Great Pyramid?
questions.a: Thousands of organized laborers and skilled workers, many paid and housed in nearby villages — not mainly slaves.

days.guide: Weigh slices; give the quiz.

questions.q: What does the Weighing of the Heart show about Egyptian ethics?
questions.a: Living honestly and doing right mattered for the afterlife.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab notes: starting and ending masses, observation that the salted slice lost more mass and resisted rot because salt/baking soda draw out water (as natron did). Quiz: 1) pharaoh was seen as a god-king 2) social pyramid: pharaoh, priests/nobles, scribes, artisans/merchants, farmers, enslaved people 3) Weighing of the Heart — heart weighed against the feather of Ma'at 4) Great Pyramid built for Khufu around 2560 BCE 5) built by organized, paid workers.

weeks.prep: Gather: hieroglyph alphabet chart, paper bag (for papyrus effect), images of Abu Simbel and Deir el-Bahri. Print a hieroglyph alphabet; find Abu Simbel and Deir el-Bahri images.
misconceptions: Thinking hieroglyphs are just pictures. They combine sound signs and meaning signs.
Accepting royal monuments as unbiased. They are often propaganda.

days.guide: Learn how the Rosetta Stone was deciphered; write name in a cartouche.

questions.q: Why was the Rosetta Stone the key to hieroglyphs?
questions.a: It had the same text in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek; scholars like Champollion used the Greek to decipher the hieroglyphs (1822).

days.guide: Analyze art rules; draw in Egyptian style.

questions.q: What is hierarchical scale?
questions.a: Showing more important people larger.

days.guide: Read about Hatshepsut.

questions.q: What was notable about Hatshepsut's reign?
questions.a: She ruled as pharaoh, sent a trading expedition to Punt and built a great temple at Deir el-Bahri; later rulers erased many of her images.

days.guide: Examine Kadesh accounts.

questions.q: Why is Ramses II's Kadesh account considered propaganda?
questions.a: He presented the battle as a great victory, but it was likely a draw and later ended with a peace treaty with the Hittites.

days.guide: The child writes the comparison.

questions.q: What is a cartouche?
questions.a: An oval around a royal name in hieroglyphs.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison paragraph — 4: compares Hatshepsut (female pharaoh, peaceful trade expedition to Punt, temple at Deir el-Bahri; images later erased) and Ramses II (long reign, building projects like Abu Simbel, military campaigns like Kadesh presented as a great victory, later peace treaty with the Hittites), with evidence and an evaluation of legacy; 3: both described, little comparison; 2: one ruler; 1: inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Gather: map of Egypt and Kush, images of Meroe pyramids. Print a map of Egypt and Kush and images of Meroë's pyramids.
misconceptions: Thinking Kush was just a part of Egypt. It was a powerful independent kingdom that even ruled Egypt.
Thinking all pyramids are in Egypt. Kush built more pyramids (at Meroë and Napata) than Egypt.

days.guide: Map trade with Punt, Nubia, the Levant and Crete.

questions.q: What did Egypt get from Nubia?
questions.a: Gold, ivory, ebony and other goods.

days.guide: Read about Kush and Piye.

questions.q: Who was Piye?
questions.a: A king of Kush who conquered Egypt and founded the 25th Dynasty.

days.guide: Compare Meroë and Giza pyramids.

questions.q: Why was Meroë a strong economic center?
questions.a: It had iron ore and wood for fuel, making it a major ironworking and trading center.

days.guide: Make the Egypt–Kush timeline.

questions.q: Give an example of cultural borrowing between Kush and Egypt.
questions.a: Kush built pyramids and worshipped Egyptian gods like Amun.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test.

questions.q: Where was Kush located?
questions.a: South of Egypt along the Nile, in Nubia (modern Sudan).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test sample: Nile geography; Narmer; pharaoh; afterlife beliefs; Great Pyramid; Rosetta Stone; Hatshepsut; Ramses II; Kush in Nubia south of Egypt, rich in gold, ivory and ebony; Piye conquered Egypt (~728 BCE, 25th Dynasty); Meroë famous for ironworking; Meroë pyramids smaller and steeper than Giza.

weeks.prep: Gather: map of ancient Canaan and Egypt, Hebrew Bible excerpts: Genesis 12 and Exodus 20. Print Genesis 12 and Exodus 20. Approach religious texts as historical and cultural sources; respect your family's beliefs while noting what is tradition vs. archaeology.
misconceptions: Thinking monotheism was common. Most ancient peoples were polytheistic.
Confusing Hebrews, Israelites and Jews. Explain how the names developed over time.

days.guide: Map Abraham's journey.

questions.q: Where did Abraham's journey begin and end according to Genesis?
questions.a: From Ur in Mesopotamia to Canaan.

days.guide: Compare monotheism and polytheism.

questions.q: Why is Judaism's monotheism historically significant?
questions.a: It was one of the earliest lasting monotheistic faiths and influenced Christianity and Islam.

days.guide: Read the Exodus account; map the route.

questions.q: What does Passover commemorate?
questions.a: The Exodus — the Israelites' liberation from slavery in Egypt.

days.guide: Categorize the commandments.

questions.q: Give one commandment about duties to people.
questions.a: Honor your father and mother; do not murder; do not steal; do not bear false witness.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What is monotheism?
questions.a: Belief in one God.

weeks.assessment_key: Map: Ur to Haran to Canaan; Egypt and the Sinai. Quiz: 1) Abraham is considered the founder of the Hebrew people (journey from Ur to Canaan in Genesis) 2) monotheism = belief in one God 3) Moses led the Exodus from Egypt 4) Passover commemorates the Exodus 5) Ten Commandments: duties to God (first commandments) and to people (honor parents, do not kill, steal, lie or covet).

weeks.prep: Gather: Book of Ruth (short reading), excerpts from the prophets (Micah 6:8, Amos 5:24). Read the Book of Ruth (4 short chapters) and Micah 6:8, Amos 5:24.
misconceptions: Thinking the prophets predicted the future mainly. They also called for justice and ethical behavior.
Thinking ethics are separate from law. In Jewish tradition they were linked.

days.guide: Read Ruth; discuss loyalty.

questions.q: What does Ruth teach about loyalty and kindness?
questions.a: Ruth stays with her mother-in-law Naomi ('Where you go I will go'), and Boaz treats her, a foreigner, kindly — valuing loyalty and kindness to strangers.

days.guide: Read about David and Solomon; add to timeline.

questions.q: What did Solomon build?
questions.a: The First Temple in Jerusalem.

days.guide: Read Micah and Amos.

questions.q: Explain Micah 6:8 in your own words.
questions.a: God wants people to act justly, love kindness/mercy and be humble.

days.guide: Connect teachings to Western traditions.

questions.q: Name one Jewish teaching that influenced later Western traditions.
questions.a: A weekly day of rest (Sabbath), care for the poor, the idea that even rulers are under law.

days.guide: The child writes the paragraph.

questions.q: Who was David?
questions.a: A king of Israel who made Jerusalem the capital.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric — 4: clear topic sentence answering the question, at least two specific accurate pieces of evidence (named source, artifact or fact), explanation linking each to the claim, concluding sentence; 3: accurate but only one piece of evidence explained; 2: general statements without evidence; 1: inaccurate or off-topic. Expected: e.g., justice — Micah 6:8 ('do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with your God') and Amos 5:24 ('let justice roll down like waters') — influenced Western ideas that leaders must be just and that the poor deserve care; or the Sabbath as weekly rest.

weeks.prep: Gather: map of the Mediterranean and Near East, image of the Arch of Titus. Print a Near East/Mediterranean map and the Arch of Titus relief image.
misconceptions: Thinking the Jewish people disappeared after 70 CE. They maintained their faith through study, synagogues and communities across the Diaspora.
Confusing the First and Second Temples.

days.guide: Read about the Babylonian exile; map.

questions.q: Who destroyed the First Temple, and when?
questions.a: The Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar, in 586 BCE.

days.guide: Read about Cyrus and the Second Temple.

questions.q: Why did Cyrus let the Jews return?
questions.a: Persian policy tolerated local religions; Cyrus allowed exiles to return and rebuild.

days.guide: Analyze the Arch of Titus.

questions.q: What does the Arch of Titus show?
questions.a: Roman soldiers carrying treasures, including the menorah, from the Temple after its destruction in 70 CE.

days.guide: Read about Yavneh.

questions.q: How did Judaism survive without the Temple?
questions.a: Through study of Torah, synagogues, rabbis and communities across the Diaspora; Yavneh became a center of learning.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test.

questions.q: What is the Diaspora?
questions.a: The scattering of Jewish communities outside the land of Israel.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test sample: Abraham; monotheism; Exodus; Ten Commandments; David and Solomon; Babylonians destroyed the First Temple (586 BCE) and exiled many Jews; Cyrus of Persia allowed return (539 BCE); Second Temple rebuilt; Romans destroyed it in 70 CE; Arch of Titus shows the menorah taken; Yohanan ben Zakkai's academy at Yavneh; Diaspora = scattering of Jews outside their homeland (map shows communities in Babylon, Egypt, Asia Minor, Rome).

weeks.prep: Gather: relief map of Greece, clay or salt dough. Make salt dough (2 cups flour, 1 cup salt, ~¾ cup water) and print a relief map of Greece.
misconceptions: Thinking Greece was one unified country. It was many independent city-states.
Thinking the Minoans and Mycenaeans were the same.

days.guide: Make the relief map.

questions.q: What percent of Greece is mountainous?
questions.a: About three-quarters (roughly 75–80%).

days.guide: Diagram a polis.

questions.q: What were the acropolis and agora?
questions.a: Acropolis — the high, fortified hill with temples; agora — the marketplace and meeting place.

days.guide: Compare Minoans and Mycenaeans.

questions.q: How were the Minoans and Mycenaeans different?
questions.a: Minoans (Crete, palace of Knossos) were sea traders; Mycenaeans (mainland) were warriors with fortified citadels.

days.guide: Map Greek colonies.

questions.q: Why did Greeks start colonies?
questions.a: Limited farmland and growing population; to trade.

days.guide: The child writes the paragraph.

questions.q: How did mountains shape Greek government?
questions.a: They separated communities, so each developed as an independent city-state.

weeks.assessment_key: Map: mountains, peninsula, islands, Aegean and Ionian Seas. Paragraph rubric — 4: clear topic sentence answering the question, at least two specific accurate pieces of evidence (named source, artifact or fact), explanation linking each to the claim, concluding sentence; 3: accurate but only one piece of evidence explained; 2: general statements without evidence; 1: inaccurate or off-topic. Expected: mountains separated communities → independent poleis; little farmland → trade and colonies; the sea → skilled sailors.

weeks.prep: Gather: pottery shards or paper ostraka, excerpt of Pericles' Funeral Oration (Thucydides). Cut paper ostraka; print an excerpt of Pericles' Funeral Oration.
misconceptions: Thinking all Athenians could vote. Only free adult male citizens; women, enslaved people and foreigners couldn't.
Thinking the U.S. is a direct democracy. It's a representative democracy (republic).

days.guide: Chart forms of government.

questions.q: What is an oligarchy? Give a Greek example.
questions.a: Rule by a few powerful people; Sparta.

days.guide: Read about Solon and Cleisthenes.

questions.q: Who could participate in Athenian democracy?
questions.a: Free adult men born to Athenian citizens; not women, enslaved people or foreigners.

days.guide: Hold the mock ostracism.

questions.q: What was ostracism?
questions.a: A vote to exile a citizen thought dangerous to democracy for ten years.

days.guide: Read the Funeral Oration excerpt.

questions.q: Name a value Pericles praised.
questions.a: Equality before the law, rule by the many, advancement by merit, citizen participation.

days.guide: The child writes the comparison; quiz.

questions.q: What is direct democracy?
questions.a: Citizens vote on laws themselves.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison essay — 4: explains Athenian direct democracy (citizens voted on laws in the Assembly) vs. U.S. representative democracy (elected representatives), who participated in each, with examples; 3: accurate but thin; 2: one side; 1: inaccurate. Quiz: monarchy (one ruler, inherited), aristocracy (nobles), oligarchy (a few rich/powerful — Sparta), tyranny (one ruler who seized power), democracy (rule by citizens — Athens).

weeks.prep: Gather: map of the Persian Empire, Herodotus excerpts on Marathon and Thermopylae. Print a Persian Empire map and Herodotus excerpts.
misconceptions: Thinking Herodotus is perfectly reliable. He was Greek, so he may favor Greeks and exaggerate Persian numbers.
Thinking the 300 Spartans fought alone at Thermopylae. Thousands of allied Greeks fought there too.

days.guide: Complete the Athens–Sparta chart.

questions.q: How did Spartan education differ from Athenian?
questions.a: Spartan boys trained for the military from age 7; Athenian boys studied subjects like reading, music and athletics.

days.guide: Map the Persian Empire.

questions.q: What was the Royal Road?
questions.a: A long road (about 1,600 miles from Sardis to Susa) with relay stations to speed messages and trade.

days.guide: Read Herodotus; evaluate bias.

questions.q: Why might Herodotus be biased?
questions.a: He was Greek writing about Greek victories and may have exaggerated Persian numbers.

days.guide: Diagram Salamis.

questions.q: How did the Greeks win at Salamis?
questions.a: Themistocles lured the large Persian fleet into a narrow strait where faster Greek triremes could ram them.

days.guide: Give the cumulative quiz.

questions.q: Who won the Battle of Marathon?
questions.a: The Athenians (490 BCE).

weeks.assessment_key: Semester 1 cumulative quiz sample: 1) primary vs. secondary 2) Beringia 3) farming → surplus → specialization 4) cuneiform 5) Hammurabi's Code 6) Nile flows north 7) Rosetta Stone 8) Kush/Meroë iron 9) monotheism 10) polis 11) Cleisthenes 12) Marathon 490 BCE, Thermopylae and Salamis 480 BCE.

weeks.prep: Gather: images of the Parthenon, Thucydides excerpt on the plague. Print Parthenon images and a short Thucydides excerpt on the plague (preview: it describes disease vividly).
misconceptions: Thinking the Golden Age benefited all Greeks. Athens used Delian League funds for its own buildings, angering allies.
Thinking Athens won the war. Sparta won in 404 BCE.

days.guide: Read about Pericles' Athens; list achievements.

questions.q: Whom did the Parthenon honor?
questions.a: Athena, patron goddess of Athens.

days.guide: Explain the Delian League's transformation.

questions.q: How did the Delian League become an Athenian empire?
questions.a: Athens moved the treasury to Athens, used the money for its own projects and forced members to stay.

days.guide: Read Thucydides on the plague.

questions.q: How did the plague affect Athens in the war?
questions.a: It killed many people, including Pericles, weakening Athens' army and morale.

days.guide: Make the chart.

questions.q: What was a major result of the Peloponnesian War?
questions.a: A weakened Greece, later conquered by Macedonia.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: Who won the Peloponnesian War?
questions.a: Sparta.

weeks.assessment_key: Cause-effect chart: causes — Athens turned the Delian League into an empire, Sparta feared Athenian power; events — war began 431 BCE, plague struck Athens (430 BCE) and killed Pericles (429 BCE); effects — Sparta won (404 BCE), Greek city-states weakened, later conquered by Macedonia. Quiz: Parthenon honored Athena; Pericles led Athens; Delian League; Thucydides wrote the war's history.

weeks.prep: Gather: Aesop's Fables (Project Gutenberg), photos of Doric, Ionic and Corinthian columns. Download Aesop's Fables; walk your neighborhood or look online for columns.
misconceptions: Thinking the Olympics honored athletes alone. They honored Zeus.
Mixing up column styles.

days.guide: Read about gods and festivals.

questions.q: Whom did the ancient Olympic Games honor, and when did they begin?
questions.a: Zeus; traditionally 776 BCE at Olympia.

days.guide: Read five fables; write morals and a new fable.

questions.q: What is the moral of 'The Tortoise and the Hare'?
questions.a: Slow and steady wins the race.

days.guide: Learn theater parts; make a mask.

questions.q: What is the difference between tragedy and comedy?
questions.a: Tragedy shows a hero's downfall; comedy is humorous with a happy ending.

days.guide: Identify columns.

questions.q: How can you tell Doric, Ionic and Corinthian columns apart?
questions.a: Doric — plain top; Ionic — scroll-shaped top; Corinthian — decorated with leaves.

days.guide: List 10 Greek-origin words/brands.

questions.q: Where does the brand name Nike come from?
questions.a: Nike, the Greek goddess of victory.

weeks.assessment_key: Fable rubric — 4: animal characters, brief plot, clear stated moral; 3: moral unclear; 2: no moral; 1: incomplete. Legacy list examples: Nike (goddess of victory), marathon (battle of Marathon), Olympics, panic (Pan), echo, Atlas (maps), Amazon, Midas touch, Achilles' heel/tendon, Pandora, Trident, Hercules, Apollo program.

weeks.prep: Gather: Plato's Apology excerpt, map of Alexander's empire, compass and straightedge. Print an excerpt of Plato's Apology and Alexander's empire map; get a compass and straightedge.
misconceptions: Thinking Socrates wrote books. Plato recorded his ideas.
Thinking Alexander only conquered. He also spread Greek culture (Hellenistic Age).

days.guide: Read about the three philosophers; question a family member on fairness.

questions.q: What is the Socratic method?
questions.a: Asking a series of questions to examine ideas and find truth.

days.guide: Research four scientists; make trading cards.

questions.q: What is Hippocrates known for?
questions.a: Treating illness as having natural causes; the Hippocratic Oath.

days.guide: Map Alexander's conquests.

questions.q: How far did Alexander's empire reach?
questions.a: From Greece and Egypt across Persia to the Indus River in India.

days.guide: Read about Alexandria; do a construction (e.g., bisect a line segment).

questions.q: What was the Library of Alexandria?
questions.a: A great center of learning with many scrolls in Egypt's city of Alexandria.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test.

questions.q: Who was Aristotle's famous student?
questions.a: Alexander the Great.

weeks.assessment_key: Trading cards: Euclid — geometry (Elements); Archimedes — levers, buoyancy, 'Eureka'; Hippocrates — medicine, Hippocratic Oath; Hypatia — mathematician and teacher in Alexandria. Unit 5 test sample: geography; polis; forms of government; Athens vs. Sparta; Persian Wars; Golden Age; Peloponnesian War; Socrates, Plato, Aristotle; Alexander; columns.

weeks.prep: Gather: map of South Asia, images of Mohenjo-daro and Indus seals. Print a South Asia map and images of Mohenjo-daro and Indus seals.
misconceptions: Thinking the Indus script has been read. It hasn't — no bilingual text exists and inscriptions are very short.
Accepting the old 'Aryan invasion destroyed the cities' theory as fact. Evidence points more to environmental change.

days.guide: Map rivers, mountains, plateau; explain monsoons.

questions.q: What are monsoons?
questions.a: Seasonal winds; summer monsoons bring heavy rain, winter monsoons are dry.

days.guide: Study Mohenjo-daro's plan.

questions.q: Give two pieces of evidence that Mohenjo-daro was planned.
questions.a: Grid streets, covered drains, standardized bricks, the Great Bath.

days.guide: Examine seals.

questions.q: Why can't scholars read the Indus script?
questions.a: No bilingual text like the Rosetta Stone, and inscriptions are very short.

days.guide: Evaluate decline theories.

questions.q: Which decline theory is best supported?
questions.a: Most scholars favor environmental change — shifting rivers and weaker monsoons.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: Name two cities of the Indus Valley civilization.
questions.a: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Indus and Ganges rivers; Himalayas; Deccan Plateau 2) monsoons — summer winds bring heavy rain, winter winds dry 3) Harappa and Mohenjo-daro 4) planning: grid streets, covered drains, standardized bricks and weights, Great Bath 5) script undeciphered. Evaluation — 4: explains three theories (climate change/weaker monsoons, rivers shifting or drying, floods/overused land, outdated invasion theory), chooses one with evidence.

weeks.prep: Gather: Rig Veda Hymn of Creation excerpt, Bhagavad Gita excerpt. Print the Rig Veda 'Hymn of Creation' (10.129) and a short Bhagavad Gita excerpt. Teach respectfully — Hinduism is a living faith.
misconceptions: Thinking Hinduism has one founder. It developed over centuries from Vedic traditions.
Thinking the varna system is unchanged today. Caste discrimination is illegal in modern India, though effects remain.

days.guide: Read about Indo-Aryan migrations and the Vedas.

questions.q: In what language were the Vedas composed?
questions.a: Sanskrit.

days.guide: Read the Hymn of Creation.

questions.q: What makes the Hymn of Creation unusual?
questions.a: It asks questions about how the universe began and ends by wondering whether anyone truly knows.

days.guide: Make the beliefs organizer.

questions.q: What is karma?
questions.a: The idea that one's actions affect one's future lives.

days.guide: Diagram varnas and jatis.

questions.q: Name the four varnas.
questions.a: Brahmins (priests), Kshatriyas (rulers/warriors), Vaishyas (merchants/farmers), Shudras (laborers/servants).

days.guide: The child writes the paragraph.

questions.q: What is moksha?
questions.a: Release from the cycle of rebirth, uniting with Brahman.

weeks.assessment_key: Organizer: Brahman (universal spirit), karma (actions have consequences), dharma (duty), reincarnation (rebirth), moksha (release from the cycle). Paragraph rubric — 4: clear topic sentence answering the question, at least two specific accurate pieces of evidence (named source, artifact or fact), explanation linking each to the claim, concluding sentence; 3: accurate but only one piece of evidence explained; 2: general statements without evidence; 1: inaccurate or off-topic. Expected: Vedic rituals led by Brahmin priests developed, through the Upanishads and later texts like the Bhagavad Gita, into Hinduism with beliefs in Brahman, karma, dharma and moksha.

weeks.prep: Gather: Dhammapada excerpts (Fordham Sourcebook), map of Asia. Print Dhammapada verses (Fordham).
misconceptions: Thinking the Buddha is worshipped as a god. He is honored as an enlightened teacher.
Thinking the Middle Way means doing nothing. It avoids extremes of luxury and harsh self-denial.

days.guide: Storyboard Siddhartha's life.

questions.q: What were the Four Sights?
questions.a: An old man, a sick man, a dead body and a holy man.

days.guide: Explain the Four Noble Truths and Eightfold Path.

questions.q: State the Four Noble Truths simply.
questions.a: Life involves suffering; suffering comes from desire/craving; ending desire ends suffering; the Eightfold Path leads there.

days.guide: Read Dhammapada verses.

questions.q: Explain 'Hatred does not cease by hatred, but only by love.'
questions.a: Revenge keeps hatred going; only kindness ends it.

days.guide: Map the spread of Buddhism.

questions.q: How did Buddhism reach Sri Lanka?
questions.a: Missionaries sent by Emperor Ashoka (including his son Mahinda).

days.guide: Make the Venn; quiz.

questions.q: What is the Middle Way?
questions.a: A balanced life avoiding extremes of luxury and self-denial.

weeks.assessment_key: Venn: both from India, belief in karma and rebirth; Hinduism — many deities/Brahman, varna system; Buddhism — founded by Siddhartha, Four Noble Truths, rejects caste ranking. Quiz: 1) Four Sights: old man, sick man, dead body, holy man 2) enlightenment under the Bodhi tree 3) Four Noble Truths 4) Eightfold Path 5) Middle Way 6) Ashoka sent missionaries to Sri Lanka.

weeks.prep: Gather: Rock Edicts of Ashoka excerpts, images of the Lion Capital of Ashoka. Print three Rock Edicts of Ashoka and an image of the Lion Capital.
misconceptions: Thinking Ashoka was always peaceful. He turned to Buddhism after the bloody Kalinga war.
Thinking 'Hindu-Arabic numerals' came from Arabia. They developed in India and spread through Arab scholars.

days.guide: Map the Maurya Empire.

questions.q: Who founded the Maurya Empire?
questions.a: Chandragupta Maurya.

days.guide: Read three edicts.

questions.q: What values did Ashoka promote?
questions.a: Nonviolence, religious tolerance, respect for elders, kindness to animals, public welfare.

days.guide: Analyze the Lion Capital.

questions.q: Where does Ashoka's legacy appear in modern India?
questions.a: The Lion Capital is India's national emblem (on currency); the Ashoka Chakra wheel is on the flag.

days.guide: Research and chart achievements.

questions.q: Name an important Indian math contribution.
questions.a: Zero as a number and the place-value decimal numerals we use today.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test.

questions.q: What war changed Ashoka?
questions.a: The Kalinga war.

weeks.assessment_key: Edict analysis — 4: identifies values (nonviolence, tolerance of all religions, respect for parents, kindness to animals, care for people's welfare) with quotes and links to remorse after Kalinga. Unit 6 test sample: geography and monsoons; Harappan cities; Vedas; varnas; Hindu beliefs; Buddha; Maurya Empire founded by Chandragupta Maurya (~321 BCE); Ashoka's edicts; the Ashoka Chakra on India's flag and the Lion Capital as the national emblem; zero and decimal numerals.

weeks.prep: Gather: map of China, images of oracle bones and Shang bronzes. Print a China map with deserts, mountains and rivers; find oracle bone images.
misconceptions: Thinking China was isolated by choice. Natural barriers limited contact.
Thinking oracle bones were just decoration. They were used to ask ancestors questions — and are the earliest Chinese writing.

days.guide: Label barriers and rivers.

questions.q: How did geography isolate China?
questions.a: Mountains, deserts and the ocean surrounded it, limiting contact.

days.guide: Discuss 'China's Sorrow'.

questions.q: Why was the Huang He called 'China's Sorrow'?
questions.a: Its floods killed many people and destroyed farms.

days.guide: Study oracle bones; write a question.

questions.q: How were oracle bones used?
questions.a: Questions were carved on bones or shells; heated until they cracked, and priests read the cracks as answers.

days.guide: Analyze bronzes.

questions.q: What do Shang bronzes show?
questions.a: Advanced metalworking skill and the importance of ancestor rituals.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What is loess?
questions.a: Fine, fertile yellow soil.

weeks.assessment_key: Map: Himalayas, Gobi and Taklamakan deserts, Pacific Ocean, Huang He and Chang Jiang. Quiz: 1) barriers isolated China 2) Huang He called 'China's Sorrow' for deadly floods 3) loess = fertile yellow soil 4) Shang oracle bones were heated until they cracked and the cracks interpreted 5) bronze vessels used in ancestor rituals.

weeks.prep: Gather: Analects of Confucius excerpts, Dao De Jing excerpts. Print 10 Analects sayings and Dao De Jing passages.
misconceptions: Thinking the Mandate of Heaven was permanent. It could be lost by bad rulers.
Thinking Confucianism and Daoism agree on government. Confucians wanted active virtuous leaders; Daoists wanted minimal government.

days.guide: Draw the dynastic cycle.

questions.q: What was the Mandate of Heaven?
questions.a: The belief that heaven grants the right to rule to a just ruler and takes it away from an unjust one.

days.guide: Read about the Warring States.

questions.q: What problems did Confucius see?
questions.a: Disorder, warfare, corrupt rulers and people neglecting duties.

days.guide: Read Analects sayings.

questions.q: Name the five relationships.
questions.a: Ruler–subject, father–son, husband–wife, older brother–younger brother, friend–friend.

days.guide: Read the Dao De Jing.

questions.q: How does Daoism view government?
questions.a: The best government does little and lets things follow their natural course.

days.guide: The child writes the dialogue.

questions.q: What is filial piety?
questions.a: Respect and duty toward parents and ancestors.

weeks.assessment_key: Dialogue rubric — 4: Confucius stresses virtuous rulers, proper relationships, filial piety and education; Laozi stresses harmony with nature, simplicity and governing little (wu wei); both use accurate ideas and respond to each other; 3: accurate, one-sided; 2: inaccurate in places; 1: off-topic.

weeks.prep: Gather: images of the terracotta army, clay. Find terracotta army images; have air-dry clay.
misconceptions: Thinking the Great Wall was built all at once. Qin linked earlier walls; most of today's wall is from the Ming dynasty.
Seeing Shi Huangdi as only good or only bad.

days.guide: Read about unification; list standardizations.

questions.q: Name three things Shi Huangdi standardized.
questions.a: Writing, coins, weights and measures, axle widths.

days.guide: Compare Legalism and Confucianism.

questions.q: What did Legalists believe?
questions.a: People are selfish, so strict laws and harsh punishments are needed.

days.guide: Map early walls; discuss workers.

questions.q: What was the cost of the Great Wall?
questions.a: Forced labor; many workers died.

days.guide: Study the terracotta army; sculpt a soldier.

questions.q: What is the terracotta army?
questions.a: Thousands of life-size clay soldiers buried near Shi Huangdi's tomb (found 1974).

days.guide: The child writes the evaluation.

questions.q: What was the 'burning of books'?
questions.a: The Qin ordered many books (especially Confucian) burned to control ideas.

weeks.assessment_key: Evaluation rubric — 4: uses evidence for 'great leader' (unified China, standardized writing, coins, weights and axle widths, built roads and walls) and 'tyrant' (Legalist harsh punishments, burned books, forced labor) and reaches a supported judgment; 3: both sides, weak conclusion; 2: one side; 1: inaccurate.

weeks.prep: Gather: map of Eurasia, paper-making supplies (scrap paper, blender, screen). Gather scrap paper, a blender (adult), and a screen for papermaking.
misconceptions: Thinking the Silk Road was one road. It was a network of routes.
Thinking only goods traveled. Ideas, religions and diseases did too.

days.guide: Read about Han exams.

questions.q: How did Confucianism shape Han government?
questions.a: Officials were chosen partly by exams on Confucian classics, valuing education and virtue.

days.guide: Make paper; list inventions.

questions.q: Name three Han inventions.
questions.a: Paper, seismograph, wheelbarrow (also the rudder).

days.guide: Map the Silk Roads.

questions.q: Name goods traveling east and west.
questions.a: West: silk, paper; east: horses, glass, wool, gold.

days.guide: Trace Buddhism to China.

questions.q: How did Buddhism reach China?
questions.a: Merchants and monks along the Silk Roads.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test.

questions.q: What was Chang'an?
questions.a: The Han capital and eastern starting point of the Silk Roads.

weeks.assessment_key: Silk Roads map: Chang'an west through Central Asia to the Mediterranean; goods east→west: silk, paper, spices; west→east: horses, glass, wool, gold/silver. Unit 7 test sample: geography; Shang; Mandate of Heaven; Confucius and Laozi; Qin Legalism and standardization; Han civil service exams based on Confucian learning; Han inventions — paper, seismograph, wheelbarrow; Silk Roads; Buddhism entered China via the Silk Roads.

weeks.prep: Gather: map of Italy, Livy's account of Romulus and Remus (excerpt). Print a map of Italy and Livy's account of Romulus and Remus.
misconceptions: Treating legends as history. Romulus and Remus is a founding myth; archaeology shows small villages on the hills.
Thinking Rome invented everything. It borrowed heavily from Etruscans and Greeks.

days.guide: Map Italy, the Tiber and the seven hills.

questions.q: Why was Rome's location good?
questions.a: Hills for defense, the Tiber for water and trade, and central position in the Mediterranean.

days.guide: Read Livy; separate legend from evidence.

questions.q: What part of the Romulus story is legend, and what does archaeology show?
questions.a: Twins raised by a she-wolf is legend; archaeology shows early villages on the Palatine Hill around the 700s BCE.

days.guide: List borrowings.

questions.q: What did Rome borrow from the Greeks?
questions.a: Gods (renamed), architecture, the alphabet (through the Etruscans), ideas in literature and philosophy.

days.guide: Read about Cincinnatus.

questions.q: Why is Cincinnatus compared to George Washington?
questions.a: Both gave up power voluntarily and returned to their farms.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What river runs through Rome?
questions.a: The Tiber.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Tiber River and seven hills 2) central Mediterranean location aided trade 3) legend: Romulus and Remus raised by a she-wolf; Romulus founded Rome (753 BCE traditionally) 4) Aeneas fled Troy 5) Etruscans: arches, engineering 6) Greeks: gods, alphabet (via Etruscans), architecture 7) Cincinnatus left his farm to lead Rome, then gave up power.

weeks.prep: Gather: Twelve Tables excerpts (Avalon or Fordham), U.S. Constitution summary. Print Twelve Tables excerpts and a U.S. Constitution summary.
misconceptions: Thinking the Roman Republic was a democracy for all. Wealthy patricians dominated, especially early.
Thinking the U.S. copied Rome exactly.

days.guide: Read about the Conflict of the Orders.

questions.q: How did plebeians gain rights?
questions.a: By refusing to work or fight (leaving the city), they won tribunes and written laws.

days.guide: Diagram the government.

questions.q: How did two consuls check each other?
questions.a: Each could veto the other's decisions.

days.guide: Read Twelve Tables laws.

questions.q: Why did written laws matter?
questions.a: Everyone could know the law, protecting plebeians from unfair judges.

days.guide: Chart Rome vs. the U.S.

questions.q: Name two U.S. features from Rome.
questions.a: The Senate, the veto, checks and balances, written laws.

days.guide: Write the paragraph; quiz.

questions.q: What does 'veto' mean in Latin?
questions.a: 'I forbid.'

weeks.assessment_key: Chart: consuls (two, one-year terms, could veto each other) ↔ president; Senate ↔ U.S. Senate; assemblies/tribunes ↔ House; written law (Twelve Tables) ↔ Constitution; veto in both. Paragraph rubric — 4: clear topic sentence answering the question, at least two specific accurate pieces of evidence (named source, artifact or fact), explanation linking each to the claim, concluding sentence; 3: accurate but only one piece of evidence explained; 2: general statements without evidence; 1: inaccurate or off-topic. Vocabulary quiz: republic, patrician, plebeian, consul, Senate, tribune, veto ('I forbid'), Twelve Tables.

weeks.prep: Gather: map of Roman expansion, Plutarch's Life of Caesar excerpt, Res Gestae of Augustus excerpt. Print excerpts from Plutarch's Life of Caesar and the Res Gestae; a map of Roman expansion.
misconceptions: Thinking Augustus called himself king. He used titles like princeps ('first citizen') while holding real power.
Thinking Caesar was emperor. He was dictator; Augustus was the first emperor.

days.guide: Map the Punic Wars and Hannibal's route.

questions.q: What did Rome gain by defeating Carthage?
questions.a: Control of the western Mediterranean.

days.guide: Read about the Gracchi and Cicero.

questions.q: What did the Gracchi try to do?
questions.a: Give land to poor citizens; they were killed by opponents in the Senate.

days.guide: Read Plutarch; debate Caesar.

questions.q: Why did crossing the Rubicon matter?
questions.a: Bringing an army into Italy broke the law and started civil war.

days.guide: Read the Res Gestae.

questions.q: How did Augustus present his power?
questions.a: As restoring the Republic and being 'first citizen', while controlling the army and government.

days.guide: Make the timeline; quiz.

questions.q: Who was the first Roman emperor?
questions.a: Augustus (27 BCE).

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline: 509 BCE Republic founded; 264–146 BCE Punic Wars; 133 BCE Tiberius Gracchus; 49 BCE Caesar crosses the Rubicon; 44 BCE Caesar assassinated; 27 BCE Augustus becomes the first emperor (beginning of the Pax Romana). Quiz: Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants; Carthage destroyed 146 BCE; the gap between rich and poor and powerful generals weakened the Republic.

weeks.prep: Gather: images of Roman coins (Smithsonian), map of Roman roads and trade, cardboard and tape for aqueduct. Print Roman coin images and road maps; gather cardboard and tape.
misconceptions: Thinking all Romans lived like the rich. Most were poor or enslaved.
Thinking aqueducts used pumps. They used gravity and a gentle slope.

days.guide: Map roads and sea routes.

questions.q: Why were Roman roads important?
questions.a: They moved armies, trade and messages quickly.

days.guide: Analyze coins.

questions.q: How did coins spread imperial messages?
questions.a: They showed the emperor's face and slogans everywhere.

days.guide: Compare rich and poor days.

questions.q: Where did poor Romans in the city often live?
questions.a: Crowded apartment buildings (insulae).

days.guide: Build the aqueduct.

questions.q: What makes an aqueduct work?
questions.a: A gentle downhill slope so gravity moves water.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What province supplied much of Rome's grain?
questions.a: Egypt.

weeks.assessment_key: Aqueduct rubric: carries water 1 m with a gentle, consistent slope (a few cm), measured drop recorded. Quiz: roads connected the empire; common coins eased trade and showed the emperor's image; goods (grain from Egypt, olive oil, wine, metals); slavery widespread; entertainment at the Colosseum and Circus Maximus.

weeks.prep: Gather: Sermon on the Mount excerpt (Matthew 5-7), map of Paul's journeys. Print Matthew 5–7 excerpts and a map of Paul's journeys; present religious content historically and respectfully.
misconceptions: Thinking Christianity was immediately accepted. It was persecuted at times before becoming legal.
Confusing the Edict of Milan with making Christianity official. Milan (313 CE) allowed it; Theodosius made it official (380 CE).

days.guide: Read about Roman rule in Judea and the revolts.

questions.q: What happened after the Jewish revolts?
questions.a: Rome destroyed the Temple (70 CE) and later banned Jews from Jerusalem after the Bar Kokhba revolt.

days.guide: Read the Sermon on the Mount.

questions.q: Name two teachings from the Sermon on the Mount.
questions.a: Love your enemies; the Beatitudes ('Blessed are the meek'); the Golden Rule.

days.guide: Map Paul's journeys.

questions.q: What was Paul's role?
questions.a: He traveled and wrote letters spreading Christianity, especially to non-Jews.

days.guide: Make the timeline.

questions.q: What was the Edict of Milan?
questions.a: Constantine's 313 CE decree allowing Christians to worship freely.

days.guide: The child writes the explanation.

questions.q: Which emperor made Christianity the official religion?
questions.a: Theodosius (380 CE).

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric — 4: clear topic sentence answering the question, at least two specific accurate pieces of evidence (named source, artifact or fact), explanation linking each to the claim, concluding sentence; 3: accurate but only one piece of evidence explained; 2: general statements without evidence; 1: inaccurate or off-topic. Expected factors: Roman roads and peace made travel easy; common languages (Greek, Latin); Paul's missionary journeys and letters; the message's appeal to the poor and enslaved; Constantine's support and the Edict of Milan; later official status under Theodosius.

weeks.prep: Gather: Latin roots list, images of the Pantheon and Colosseum. Print a Latin roots list and Pantheon/Colosseum images.
misconceptions: Thinking Rome 'fell' in one day. The decline took centuries; the West ended in 476 CE, the East continued.
Thinking 'Eureka' is Latin. It's Greek.

days.guide: Compare the Pantheon and Colosseum with modern buildings.

questions.q: Name three Roman building innovations.
questions.a: Arches, domes, concrete.

days.guide: Find Latin roots; translate mottos.

questions.q: What does 'E pluribus unum' mean?
questions.a: 'Out of many, one.'

days.guide: Identify legal principles.

questions.q: Name a Roman legal principle used today.
questions.a: Innocent until proven guilty.

days.guide: Read about the fall; rank causes.

questions.q: When did the Western Roman Empire fall?

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test.

questions.q: What does California's motto 'Eureka' mean?
questions.a: 'I have found it' (Greek).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test sample: geography; legends; Republic structure; Twelve Tables; Punic Wars; Caesar; Augustus; Pax Romana; roads, aqueducts, concrete, arches, domes; Latin roots; spread of Christianity; 476 CE fall of the West (Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus); causes: invasions, economic trouble, political instability, an overextended empire.

weeks.prep: Gather: year-long timeline, poster board or slides. Gather the year's timeline and notes; poster board or slides.
misconceptions: Choosing a legacy without tracing it across civilizations.
Not connecting to life today.

days.guide: The child chooses a legacy and plans.

questions.q: Trace 'law' across three civilizations.
questions.a: Hammurabi's Code (Babylon), Ten Commandments (Hebrews), Twelve Tables (Rome).

days.guide: Gather evidence including two primary sources.

questions.q: Name a primary source for democracy.
questions.a: Pericles' Funeral Oration.

days.guide: Create the exhibit.

questions.q: Connect Roman engineering to California today.
questions.a: Aqueducts → California Aqueduct; arches and concrete in buildings.

days.guide: Present as a docent.

questions.q: What makes a good docent?
questions.a: Clear explanations, knowledge and answering visitors' questions.

days.guide: Complete the timeline; give the final.

questions.q: Which came first: Hammurabi or Alexander?
questions.a: Hammurabi (~1750 BCE vs. ~330 BCE).

weeks.assessment_key: Legacy project rubric — 4: one legacy traced across 3+ civilizations, two primary sources, accurate details, clear connection to California today, confident docent presentation; 3: two civilizations or one source; 2: limited evidence; 1: incomplete. Cumulative final sample: one question per civilization — Mesopotamia (cuneiform, Hammurabi), Egypt (Nile, pharaohs), Kush (Meroë), Hebrews (monotheism), Greece (democracy), India (Ashoka, zero), China (Confucius, Silk Roads), Rome (Republic, law).

MATH.overview: Teach each lesson in about 60 minutes: briefly model a problem aloud, work one together, then let your child practice independently while you circulate and ask 'how do you know?'. The course follows Illustrative Mathematics Grade 6, so hands-on models (cutting shapes, tape diagrams, double number lines, balances) come before formulas — don't skip them. Use Day 5 quizzes to find gaps and reteach before moving on; insist on labeled units and written reasoning.

weeks.prep: Gather: graph paper, scissors, tangram set or paper tangrams. Print or cut paper tangrams if you have no set; draw a few tilted parallelograms on graph paper ahead of Day 4.
misconceptions: Using the slanted side as the height. Correct: height is always perpendicular (makes a square corner) to the base; check with the corner of an index card.
Thinking shapes that look different must have different areas. Show that rearranging pieces never changes area — nothing is added or removed.

days.guide: Let the child cover the square, the medium triangle and the parallelogram tangram pieces with the two small triangles. Ask: 'If both are covered by exactly the same pieces, what do you know about their areas?' Have them write two sentences explaining that area is the amount of surface covered, not the shape.

questions.q: In a standard tangram set, the square and the medium triangle can each be covered exactly by the two small triangles. Which has more area?
questions.a: Neither — they have equal area, because each is made of the same two small triangles; rearranging pieces does not change area.

days.guide: Draw an L-shape on graph paper: a 6-wide by 8-tall rectangle with a 3-wide by 4-tall piece missing from the top-right. Model one method (cut into two rectangles), then have the child do 'enclose and subtract' and 'rearrange' themselves and compare answers.

questions.q: Find the area of that L-shape (6 × 8 rectangle with a 3 × 4 corner removed) two ways.
questions.a: 36 square units. Cut apart: 3 × 8 = 24 plus 3 × 4 = 12 → 36. Enclose and subtract: 6 × 8 = 48 − 12 = 36.

days.guide: Have the child cut out a paper parallelogram, draw a height line from one top corner straight down to the base, cut along it and slide the triangle to the other side. Ask what shape it makes and what its length and width are; record A = b × h, then assign the 8 problems.

questions.q: A parallelogram has base 9 cm and height 4 cm. What is its area?
Base 7.5 m, height 2 m?
questions.a: 15 sq m.

days.guide: Show that any side can be the base, and the height is the perpendicular distance to the opposite side — sometimes drawn outside the shape with a dashed extension. Draw one tilted parallelogram and find area with both base-height pairs to show they agree.

questions.q: A parallelogram has sides 10 and 6. The height to the side of length 10 is 4.8. What is the height to the side of length 6?

days.guide: Give the 10-problem quiz (see key) without help. Afterward, have the child find any error and write one sentence naming the mistake (e.g., 'I used the slanted side instead of the height').

questions.q: Why does A = b × h work for a parallelogram?
questions.a: You can cut off a triangle from one side and move it to the other to form a rectangle with the same base and height, so its area is base × height.

weeks.assessment_key: Sample 10-problem quiz: 1) rectangle 7 × 12 = 84 sq units 2) parallelogram b = 10, h = 6 → 60 3) b = 4.5, h = 8 → 36 4) 10 × 6 rectangle with a 4 × 3 corner removed → 60 − 12 = 48 5) parallelogram area 72, base 9 → height 8 6) b = 15, h = 3.2 → 48 7) square side 9 → 81 8) parallelogram b = 20, h = 2.5 → 50 9) two rectangles 5 × 4 and 3 × 6 joined → 20 + 18 = 38 10) parallelogram area 56, height 7 → base 8. Explanation (full credit): cutting the right triangle off one end and sliding it to the other end makes a rectangle with the same base and height, so area = b × h; the height must be perpendicular to the base.

weeks.prep: Gather: paper triangles, ruler, scissors. Cut two identical triangles before Day 1 (or let the child trace and cut).
misconceptions: Using the slanted side as the height of a triangle. The height is perpendicular to the chosen base, and for obtuse triangles it may fall outside the triangle.
Forgetting to halve. Remind: a triangle is half of a parallelogram with the same base and height.

days.guide: Have the child join two identical triangles into a parallelogram. Ask: 'What is the area of the parallelogram? How much of it is one triangle?' Record A = ½ × b × h.

questions.q: A triangle has base 10 and height 6. Find its area and explain using a parallelogram.
questions.a: 30 square units. Two copies make a parallelogram with area 10 × 6 = 60; one triangle is half: 30.

days.guide: On the grid, point out that the two legs of a right triangle meet at a square corner, so one leg is the base and the other is the height. The child computes the 10 areas and writes the rule in words.

questions.q: A right triangle has legs 9 and 12 and hypotenuse 15. What is its area?
questions.a: 54 square units: ½ × 9 × 12. The hypotenuse (15) is not used.

days.guide: For an obtuse triangle, model extending the base with a dashed line and dropping a perpendicular from the top vertex. The child draws all three heights with a ruler on two triangles and checks that ½bh gives the same area each time.

questions.q: An obtuse triangle has base 8 and its height (drawn outside the triangle) is 5. Area?
questions.a: 20 square units (½ × 8 × 5).

questions.q: If another side of the same triangle is 10, what is the height to that side?
questions.a: 4, because ½ × 10 × h = 20 so h = 4.

days.guide: Model the missing-dimension problem: write ½ × 8 × h = 24, so 4h = 24 and h = 6. Then the child solves the 12 problems, checking each by plugging back in.

questions.q: Area 24 sq cm, base 8 cm. Find the height.
Area 35 sq in, height 7 in. Find the base.

days.guide: Give the mixed quiz independently. Then the child corrects mistakes and writes a short paragraph explaining one error and the fix.

questions.q: A triangle and a parallelogram both have base 12 and height 5. Compare their areas.
questions.a: Triangle 30, parallelogram 60 — the triangle is half.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) b = 6, h = 9 → 27 2) right triangle legs 5 and 8 → 20 3) b = 14, h = 3 → 21 4) area 40, base 10 → height 8 5) area 18, height 4 → base 9 6) parallelogram b = 11, h = 6 → 66 7) triangle b = 7, h = 7 → 24.5 8) obtuse triangle b = 6, outside height 5 → 15. Paragraph: names the error and shows the correct calculation.

weeks.prep: Gather: graph paper, measuring tape, home floor plan sketch. Sketch your home's floor plan or pick a room/yard to measure; have a measuring tape ready for Days 3–4.
misconceptions: Adding a triangle's full b × h instead of half when decomposing. Have the child label each piece's area before adding.
Mixing units (feet and inches) in one area calculation. Convert all measurements to feet first (e.g., 10 ft 6 in = 10.5 ft).
Rounding the number of tile boxes down. You can't buy part of a box — always round up.

days.guide: Draw a trapezoid and a kite on grid paper. Have the child split each into rectangles and triangles, label each piece's area, and add; then try a second decomposition and confirm the total matches.

questions.q: A trapezoid has parallel sides 6 and 10 and height 4. Find its area by decomposing.
questions.a: 32 square units: a 6 × 4 rectangle (24) plus two triangles whose bases total 4 with height 4 (½ × 4 × 4 = 8).

questions.q: A kite has diagonals 8 and 6. Area?
questions.a: 24 square units — two triangles each with base 8 and height 3: 12 + 12.

days.guide: Have the child cut two identical trapezoids and rotate one to form a parallelogram with base (b₁ + b₂). Guide them to discover A = ½(b₁ + b₂)h, then solve the 8 problems.

questions.q: Trapezoid with bases 5 and 9 and height 6?
questions.a: 42 square units: ½ × (5 + 9) × 6.

questions.q: Bases 3.5 and 6.5, height 4?
questions.a: 20 square units: ½ × 10 × 4.

days.guide: Measure a room together, rounding to the nearest half-foot. The child sketches it on graph paper with a scale (1 square = 1 ft), splits any L-shape into rectangles and finds total area.

questions.q: A room is 12 ft by 14 ft. Area?
questions.a: 168 square feet.

questions.q: An L-shaped room is a 10 × 12 ft section plus a 4 × 6 ft nook. Area?

days.guide: Ask: 'If each tile is 1 sq ft, how many tiles cover the room? How many boxes of 10?' Discuss rounding up for partial boxes and cut tiles for irregular edges.

questions.q: A 168 sq ft room needs 1-ft tiles sold 10 per box. How many boxes?
questions.a: 17 boxes (168 ÷ 10 = 16.8, round up).

questions.q: What about 145 sq ft?
questions.a: 15 boxes (14.5 rounds up).

days.guide: Give the 6-problem assessment independently. Then the child presents the floor plan to a family member, explaining how they decomposed the shape.

questions.q: Why might two people decompose the same polygon differently but get the same area?
questions.a: Area doesn't depend on how you cut a shape; as long as pieces don't overlap or leave gaps, the pieces' areas add to the same total.

weeks.assessment_key: Composite quiz: 1) trapezoid bases 8 and 12, height 5 → 50 2) kite with diagonals 10 and 6 → 30 3) pentagon = 6 × 6 square + triangle base 6, height 4 → 36 + 12 = 48 4) 12 × 10 rectangle minus 4 × 5 corner → 100 5) 8 × 3 rectangle with triangle on top (base 8, height 3) → 24 + 12 = 36 6) hexagon made of two trapezoids (bases 4 and 8, height 3) → 18 + 18 = 36. Floor-plan rubric: 4 = accurate measurements, labeled scale drawing, correct area with work shown, tiles/boxes rounded correctly; 3 = one small calculation error; 2 = drawing or area incomplete; 1 = little work shown.

weeks.prep: Gather: cereal box, cardstock, tape, sugar cubes or snap cubes. Preview: a net must fold into the solid with no overlaps or gaps.
misconceptions: Counting only three faces of a rectangular prism. Remind that opposite faces come in pairs: SA = 2(lw + lh + wh).
Thinking 3³ means 3 × 3 = 9 or 3 × 3. Correct: the exponent tells how many times the base is used as a factor: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27.
Confusing surface area (square units) with volume (cubic units).

days.guide: Gather 6–8 objects (box, tissue box, toy pyramid). The child sorts them into prisms (two identical parallel bases) and pyramids (one base, triangle faces meeting at a point) and fills a faces/edges/vertices table.

questions.q: How many faces, edges and vertices does a cube have? A square pyramid?
questions.a: Cube: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. Square pyramid: 5 faces, 8 edges, 5 vertices.

questions.q: Triangular prism?
questions.a: 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices.

days.guide: Cut the cereal box along edges so it lies flat. The child measures each rectangle, writes its area on it, and adds all six.

questions.q: A box is 12 in × 8 in × 2 in. What is its surface area?

days.guide: Model drawing a cube net on grid paper, then the child draws nets for a rectangular prism and a square pyramid, folds one from cardstock, and computes surface area from the net.

questions.q: A cube has edges of 5 cm. Surface area?
A square pyramid has a 4 × 4 base and triangle faces with height 5. Surface area?

days.guide: Build 2×2×2, 3×3×3 and 4×4×4 cubes and count the small cubes. Write the results as 2³ = 8, 3³ = 27, 4³ = 64, and connect s² to the area of one face and 6s² to the whole surface.

questions.q: Evaluate 4³ and find the surface area of a cube with edge 4.
questions.a: 4³ = 64; SA = 6 × 4² = 96 square units.

questions.q: Volume of a cube with edge 10?
questions.a: 1,000 cubic units.

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test without help. Afterward, the child picks two missed problems and redoes them with a written explanation.

questions.q: Which units go with surface area and which with volume?
questions.a: Surface area: square units (cm², in²). Volume: cubic units (cm³, in³).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test sample key: 1) parallelogram b = 12, h = 5 → 60 2) triangle b = 9, h = 4 → 18 3) trapezoid bases 4 and 10, h = 6 → 42 4) rectangular prism 5 × 3 × 2: SA = 2(15 + 10 + 6) = 62 sq units 5) cube with edge 7: SA = 6 × 49 = 294 sq units, V = 343 cubic units 6) 5² = 25; 2⁴ = 16 7) six squares in a cross shape fold into a cube (yes) 8) square pyramid, base 6, triangle heights 5: 36 + 4 × 15 = 96 sq units. Redo: child explains each fix in a sentence.

weeks.prep: Gather: colored counters or beans, measuring cups, drink mix or food coloring. Clear cups help for color mixing; use tablespoons of water as the 'part' unit.
misconceptions: Reversing the order of a ratio. 'Red to blue' means red first; have the child say the words while writing the numbers.
Confusing part-to-part with part-to-whole. For 3 red and 2 blue, red:blue is 3:2 but red:total is 3:5.

days.guide: Put out 5 red and 3 blue beans. Model saying the ratio three ways ('5 to 3', '5:3', 'for every 5 red there are 3 blue'), then the child writes 10 ratio sentences about different collections.

questions.q: With 5 red and 3 blue beans, write the ratio of blue to red and red to all beans.
questions.a: Blue to red = 3:5; red to all = 5:8.

days.guide: Model drawing 2 flour circles and 3 egg squares for one batch, then repeat the group to show two batches. The child draws diagrams and answers the matching questions.

questions.q: A recipe uses 2 cups flour for every 3 eggs. How much flour for 6 eggs?
questions.a: 4 cups — two batches of (2 flour, 3 eggs).

days.guide: Mix one batch (2 scoops : 1 cup) and a double batch (4 scoops : 2 cups); taste both. Ask why they taste the same.

questions.q: Is 4 scoops to 2 cups equivalent to 2 scoops to 1 cup? Why?
questions.a: Yes — both quantities were multiplied by 2, so every cup has the same amount of mix.

questions.q: How many scoops for 3 cups?
questions.a: 6 scoops.

days.guide: In clear cups, mix 1 drop : 5 tbsp water and 2 drops : 10 tbsp; then 2 drops : 5 tbsp. The child records colors in a table and explains which match.

questions.q: Will 2 drops in 5 tbsp look the same as 1 drop in 5 tbsp?
questions.a: No — it will be darker, because there is more coloring per tablespoon of water (2:5 is not equivalent to 1:5).

days.guide: Give the quiz independently, then discuss part-to-part vs. part-to-whole using the family as an example.

questions.q: A class has 7 girls and 5 boys. Write a part-to-part and a part-to-whole ratio.
questions.a: Part-to-part: girls to boys 7:5. Part-to-whole: girls to all students 7:12.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz sample: picture of 4 triangles and 6 circles. 1) triangles to circles = 4:6 (or 2:3) 2) circles to triangles = 6:4 (3:2) 3) circles to all shapes = 6:10 (3:5) 4) 'For every 3 cups flour there are 2 cups sugar' — sugar to flour = 2:3 5) part-to-part compares two parts (boys:girls); part-to-whole compares a part to the total (boys:all students). Lab rubric: 4 = data table with both ratios, observation that 1:5 and 2:10 match in color, explanation that both quantities were doubled; 3 = table and match noted, explanation thin; 2 = incomplete data; 1 = no explanation.

weeks.prep: Gather: grid paper, grocery receipts. Look for receipts showing several identical items (e.g., 3 cans).
misconceptions: Adding the same number to both quantities (3:4 → 5:6) instead of multiplying. Show with a drink recipe that adding changes the taste.
Uneven tick marks on a double number line. Both lines must use equally spaced ticks that line up.

days.guide: Model making 3:4 into 6:8 and 9:12 by multiplying both numbers by the same number. The child lists five equivalent ratios and checks the 6 lists.

questions.q: List four ratios equivalent to 3:4.
Are 3:5 and 5:7 equivalent?
questions.a: No — you can't multiply both 3 and 5 by the same number to get 5 and 7.

days.guide: Draw two parallel lines, miles on top and minutes below, with ticks at 0, 1, 2, 3... miles and 0, 15, 30, 45... minutes. The child answers the 6 questions from the diagram.

questions.q: Walking 2 miles in 30 minutes, how long for 5 miles?
questions.a: 75 minutes (15 minutes per mile).

questions.q: How far in 45 minutes?
questions.a: 3 miles.

days.guide: Find a receipt item bought in multiples (or invent: 3 cans for $2.40). The child builds a double number line for cost and quantity and finds cost of 1, 5 and 12 items.

questions.q: 3 cans cost $2.40. What do 1, 5 and 12 cans cost?

days.guide: Time the child walking 20 steps. Build a double number line (steps vs. seconds) and predict 60 and 100 steps, then test one.

questions.q: If 20 steps take 12 seconds, how long for 60 steps? 100 steps?
questions.a: 36 seconds and 60 seconds.

days.guide: Give the quiz; the child corrects errors in a different color and says what went wrong.

questions.q: Is 9:12 equivalent to 12:16?
questions.a: Yes — both simplify to 3:4.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) four ratios equivalent to 5:2 — 10:4, 15:6, 20:8, 25:10 2) Is 7:3 equivalent to 14:6? Yes (×2) 3) 7:3 and 10:6? No 4) 3 lb cost $7.50: 1 lb = $2.50, 6 lb = $15 5) 4 km in 50 min at the same pace: 12 km takes 150 min 6) 9:12 and 12:16 are equivalent (both = 3:4).

weeks.prep: Gather: graph paper, Desmos (optional). Desmos is optional for plotting on Day 2.
misconceptions: Filling a table by adding across rows inconsistently. Check each row by asking 'what did I multiply by?'
Comparing ratios by looking at only one number. Build a common row (same amount of one quantity) before comparing.

days.guide: Turn a double number line into a two-column table. Show scaling up (×3) and down (÷4) in a table, then the child fills the 8 tables.

questions.q: Flour : sugar is 4 : 3. How much sugar with 12 cups flour?
questions.a: 9 cups sugar (×3).

questions.q: How much flour with 5 cups sugar?
questions.a: 6⅔ cups (each cup of sugar goes with 4/3 cup flour; 5 × 4/3 = 20/3).

days.guide: Plot rice:water pairs (1,2), (2,4), (3,6) with rice on the x-axis. Ask what the points have in common; extend the line to (0,0).

questions.q: Rice to water is 1:2. Name another point on the line and explain why it passes through (0,0).
questions.a: (5, 10), or any (x, 2x). Zero cups of rice needs zero cups of water.

days.guide: Present two runners: A runs 400 m in 80 s, B runs 300 m in 50 s. Help the child scale both to a common row (same distance or 1 second), then write a justification.

questions.q: Which runner is faster?
questions.a: B. A runs 5 m/s; B runs 6 m/s. (At 1,200 m: A takes 240 s, B 200 s.)

days.guide: Let the child work the 6 multi-step problems, requiring a labeled table for each. Ask them to explain one table aloud.

questions.q: Lemonade uses 3 cups lemon juice for every 5 cups water. With 20 cups water, how much juice and how much lemonade total?
questions.a: 12 cups juice; 32 cups total.

days.guide: Give the quiz independently, then check the graph for labeled axes and evenly spaced scales.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) table for 2:7 — 4:14, 6:21, 10:35, 1:3.5 2) points (2,7), (4,14), (6,21) lie on a line through (0,0) 3) Paint A: 3 cups blue to 5 cups yellow; Paint B: 4 cups blue to 6 cups yellow.
