Blue per cup of yellow: A = 0.6, B ≈ 0.67, so B is bluer 4) Runner who goes 100 m in 20 s (5 m/s) is slower than one who goes 150 m in 25 s (6 m/s) 5) 3 cups lemon juice per 5 cups water: 20 cups water → 12 cups juice.

weeks.prep: Gather: paper strips, trail-mix ingredients. Substitute seeds or cereal for nuts if there are allergies.
misconceptions: Dividing the total by one of the ratio numbers instead of the total number of parts. For 2:3 with 30 students, there are 5 equal parts, so each part is 6.
Treating the ratio numbers as the actual amounts. 3:2 for 2 cups doesn't mean 3 cups nuts.

days.guide: Model: boys to girls 2:3, 30 students. Draw a tape with 2 boy boxes and 3 girl boxes; 5 boxes = 30, so each box is 6. The child solves the 8 problems with tapes.

questions.q: Boys to girls is 2:3 and there are 30 students. How many of each?
questions.a: 12 boys and 18 girls.

questions.q: Red to white paint is 4:1 and the mix is 40 liters. How much red?
questions.a: 32 liters (5 parts of 8 L; red = 4 parts).

days.guide: Before measuring, the child draws a 5-part tape for 2 cups total: 3 nuts parts, 2 raisin parts. Then measure and mix.

questions.q: Trail mix is 3:2 nuts to raisins, 2 cups total. How much of each?
questions.a: Each part = 0.4 cup: 1.2 cups nuts, 0.8 cup raisins.

days.guide: Solve one problem three ways together, then the child does the other 3 and writes which method was fastest and why.

questions.q: Which representation is often fastest when you know the total of both parts?
questions.a: The tape diagram, because it shows the total split into equal parts.

days.guide: Assign the mixed review set; spot-check one problem from each type and have the child explain a tricky one.

questions.q: There are 4 cats for every 3 dogs at a shelter and 12 more cats than dogs. How many cats?
questions.a: 48 cats (the difference of 1 part = 12; cats are 4 parts = 48, dogs 36).

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test independently; afterward the child writes a 3–4 sentence reflection on their favorite strategy.

questions.q: Blue:yellow paint is 2:3 and the batch is 15 cups. How much blue?
questions.a: 6 cups (5 parts of 3 cups; blue = 2 parts).

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test sample key: 1) 12 apples, 8 oranges: apples to oranges 12:8 = 3:2; oranges to fruit 8:20 = 2:5 2) equivalent to 4:9 — 8:18, 12:27 3) 5 lb for $8 → 15 lb for $24 4) table 3:4 → 6:8, 9:12, 15:20 5) points (3,4), (6,8) are on a line through origin 6) boys:girls 4:5, 36 students → 16 boys, 20 girls 7) blue:yellow 2:3, 15 cups total → 6 blue, 9 yellow 8) Recipe A 2 cups juice : 3 cups water vs B 3 : 5 — A is stronger (0.67 vs 0.6 juice per cup water). Reflection: names a strategy and why.

weeks.prep: Gather: ruler with inches and cm, measuring cups and a liter bottle, bathroom scale. Have a phone timer ready for Day 4; know that 1 in = 2.54 cm exactly.
misconceptions: Thinking a bigger number always means a bigger length. In smaller units (cm), the same object gets a bigger number.
Multiplying when you should divide in a conversion. Ask: 'Should the answer be more or fewer units?'

days.guide: Measure a book in inches and centimeters and a mug in cups and milliliters. Ask why the cm number is bigger; the child records and explains.

questions.q: A pencil is about 7 inches long. Will its length in centimeters be a bigger or smaller number? Why?
questions.a: Bigger (about 17.8 cm), because centimeters are smaller units, so more of them fit.

days.guide: Set up a ratio table with inches and cm (1 : 2.54). The child converts the 12 measurements, scaling the table up and down.

questions.q: Convert 12 inches to cm.
Convert 5 feet to inches, then to cm.
questions.a: 60 inches; 152.4 cm.

days.guide: Ask: 'If 4 cups make 3 servings, how much water per serving? How many servings per cup?' Divide both ways and discuss when each helps.

questions.q: Find both unit rates for 4 cups of water : 3 servings.
questions.a: 1⅓ cups per serving, and ¾ serving per cup.

questions.q: How much water for 12 servings?
questions.a: 16 cups.

days.guide: Time filling the liter bottle. The child converts seconds to minutes and finds both unit rates.

questions.q: A 1-liter bottle fills in 15 seconds. Find liters per minute and minutes per liter.
questions.a: 4 liters per minute; 0.25 (¼) minute per liter.

days.guide: Give the quiz independently and review any conversion where they multiplied instead of divided.

questions.q: Convert 50.8 cm to inches.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 3 ft = 36 in 2) 10 in = 25.4 cm 3) 50.8 cm = 20 in 4) $6 for 4 lb → $1.50 per lb and ⅔ lb per dollar 5) 150 miles in 3 hours → 50 mph 6) 2 yd = 6 ft = 72 in 7) 8 cups = 2 quarts (4 cups per quart).

weeks.prep: Gather: store flyer or online grocery prices, stopwatch, tape measure. Find prices for 6 pairs of different-size items; mark a 20-meter course outside before Day 2.
misconceptions: Dividing in the wrong order for unit price (ounces ÷ dollars instead of dollars ÷ ounces). Label units: $ per oz means $ ÷ oz.
Assuming the bigger package is always the better buy. Compute the unit price first.

days.guide: Model a table: hours 1, 2, 3 vs. miles 12, 24, 36. The child solves the 8 problems, labeling every column.

questions.q: A cyclist rides 12 mph. How far in 2.5 hours? How long to ride 42 miles?
questions.a: 30 miles; 3.5 hours.

days.guide: Time the child walking, jogging and hopping 20 m. They compute m/s = 20 ÷ seconds and rank speeds.

questions.q: If walking 20 m takes 16 seconds, what is the speed?
questions.a: 1.25 meters per second.

days.guide: For each pair, divide price by size to get a unit price; round to the nearest cent and decide.

questions.q: 18 oz cereal for $4.50 or 12 oz for $3.24 — which is the better buy?

days.guide: Let the child solve the mixed problems, then explain one to a family member using units ('pages per minute').

questions.q: A heart beats 18 times in 15 seconds. How many beats per minute?
questions.a: 72 beats per minute (18 × 4).

questions.q: 48 pages in 60 minutes is how many pages per minute?
questions.a: 0.8 page per minute.

days.guide: Give the quiz and collect the lab table.

questions.q: A car goes 195 miles in 3 hours. Speed?
questions.a: 65 miles per hour.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 12 mph for 2.5 hours → 30 miles 2) 42 miles at 12 mph → 3.5 hours 3) 18 oz for $4.50 ($0.25/oz) vs 12 oz for $3.24 ($0.27/oz) → 18 oz is the better buy 4) 300 m in 60 s → 5 m/s 5) 3 lb for $5.97 → $1.99/lb. Lab table: each trial lists distance (20 m), time and m/s = 20 ÷ time.

weeks.prep: Gather: 10 x 10 grids, store sale ads. Print several 10 × 10 grids; clip 2–3 sale ads showing percent-off deals.
misconceptions: Thinking percents can't exceed 100. 120% means 1.2 times the whole — show two grids.
Finding the discount but forgetting to subtract it to get the sale price.

days.guide: Shade 25 squares of a 10 × 10 grid and say '25 out of 100 = 25% = 0.25 = ¼'. The child shades 40%, 7% and 120% (one full grid plus 20 squares).

questions.q: Write 25% as a fraction and a decimal.
What does 120% of a quantity mean?
questions.a: 1.2 times it — the whole plus 20% more.

days.guide: Teach 10% by dividing by 10, 50% by halving, 25% by halving twice, 75% as 3 × 25%. Practice with a double number line 0–100%.

questions.q: Find 10% of 80, 25% of 60 and 75% of 40.

days.guide: Model 35% of $80 = 10% ($8) × 3 + 5% ($4) = $28, and with a table. The child solves the 10 problems.

questions.q: Find 35% of $80 and 15% of 60 minutes.
questions.a: $28 and 9 minutes.

days.guide: Use real ads: find the discount, then subtract. Then compute a 15% tip as 10% + 5%.

questions.q: A $45 shirt is 20% off. Sale price?
questions.a: $36 (discount $9).

questions.q: 15% tip on a $32 bill?

days.guide: Give the percent quiz independently.

questions.q: What is 120% of 50?

weeks.prep: Gather: phone or tablet battery indicator, nutrition labels. Pick 2–3 food packages whose labels list total carbohydrates and sugars.
misconceptions: Multiplying the part by the percent instead of finding the whole. Use a tape: if 30% is 12, then 10% is 4 and 100% is 40.
Writing 'what percent' answers as a fraction or decimal without converting to per 100.

days.guide: Model '12 is 30% of what?' with a tape of 10 boxes (10% each): 3 boxes = 12, so 1 box = 4 and 10 boxes = 40. The child solves 10 problems.

questions.q: 12 is 30% of what number?
45 is 75% of what number?

days.guide: Pick a label and find, e.g., sugar as a percent of total carbohydrates: part ÷ whole × 100.

questions.q: A snack has 9 g sugar out of 36 g carbohydrates. What percent is sugar?

days.guide: Use the device: 'If 40% battery lasts 8 hours, how long would 100% last?' and download bars 'how many MB at 25%?'

questions.q: A phone at 40% has 8 hours left. How long would a full charge last at that rate?
questions.a: 20 hours.

questions.q: A 600 MB download is 25% done. How many MB have downloaded?

days.guide: Assign the mixed review and check the child labels units on every answer.

questions.q: A runner goes 3 miles in 27 minutes. Minutes per mile?
questions.a: 9 minutes per mile.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test; the child corrects missed problems.

questions.q: 18 is what percent of 72?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test sample key: 1) 12 is 30% of 40 2) 45 is 75% of 60 3) 9 is what percent of 36? 25% 4) 5 lb for $7.50 → $1.50/lb 5) 6 ft = 72 in 6) 300 miles in 5 hours = 60 mph; 210 miles at that speed takes 3.5 h 7) 40% of 85 = 34 8) a $60 jacket at 25% off = $45 9) 16 oz for $4 vs 24 oz for $5.52: $0.25 vs $0.23 per oz → 24 oz better.

weeks.prep: Gather: fraction strips, measuring cups. Check your measuring-cup set includes ¼ cup; a ¾ cup can be made with ½ + ¼.
misconceptions: Believing division always makes a number smaller. Dividing by a number less than 1 gives a quotient larger than the dividend.
Ignoring the remainder as a fraction of a group: in 2 ÷ ¾ the leftover ½ is ⅔ of a ¾-group, not ½.

days.guide: Write 12 ÷ 6, 12 ÷ 3, 12 ÷ 1, 12 ÷ ½. Have the child predict, compute, and state the pattern.

questions.q: What is 12 ÷ ½? Why is it bigger than 12?
questions.a: 24. There are two halves in each whole, so 24 halves in 12. Dividing by a number less than 1 gives a quotient greater than the dividend.

days.guide: Model two stories for 6 ÷ 2: '6 cookies, 2 per bag — how many bags?' and '6 cookies into 2 bags — how many per bag?'. The child writes and draws both.

questions.q: Write a 'how many groups' story for 6 ÷ 2.
questions.a: Example: 6 feet of rope cut into 2-foot pieces — how many pieces? 3.

days.guide: Fill a 3-cup container with ¼-cup scoops, counting; then with ¾-cup scoops.

questions.q: How many ¼ cups are in 3 cups? How many ¾ cups?

days.guide: Draw a tape of 2 wholes split into fourths; circle groups of ¾. Show 2 full groups and ⅔ of another.

questions.a: 2⅔ — two full groups of ¾ use 1½, and the leftover ½ is ⅔ of a ¾-group.

days.guide: Give the matching quiz independently.

questions.q: How many ⅓-cup scoops are in 2 cups?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (match equation–diagram–story): 1) 3 ÷ ¼ = 12 2) 3 ÷ ¾ = 4 3) 2 ÷ ¾ = 2⅔ 4) 6 ÷ ½ = 12 5) 'How many ⅓-cup scoops in 2 cups?' → 2 ÷ ⅓ = 6 6) '5 lb shared equally into 2 bags' → 5 ÷ 2 = 2½ lb each 7) 1½ ÷ ½ = 3.

weeks.prep: Gather: fraction strips, grid paper. Work 2/3 ÷ 1/6 yourself with fraction strips before Day 4 so you can model it.
misconceptions: Flipping the first fraction (dividend) instead of the divisor. Only the divisor is replaced by its reciprocal: a/b ÷ c/d = a/b × d/c.
Forgetting to convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before using the reciprocal.

days.guide: Model: '¾ lb fills ½ bag; how much fills the whole bag?' Draw a tape: half the bag = ¾, so the whole = 2 × ¾ = 1½. The child solves 6 problems with tapes.

questions.q: ¾ pound fills ½ a bag. How much fills a whole bag?
questions.a: 1½ pounds.

questions.q: 2½ liters fills ⅚ of a tank. How much fills the whole tank?
questions.a: 3 liters (each sixth holds ½ L).

days.guide: Compute 2 ÷ ⅓ (6), 5 ÷ ⅓ (15) and compare with 2 × 3 and 5 × 3. The child tests 10 examples and states the pattern.

questions.q: What is 5 ÷ ⅓? What is the shortcut?
questions.a: 15. Dividing by ⅓ is the same as multiplying by 3.

days.guide: Teach: keep the first fraction, multiply by the reciprocal of the second. Show checking: quotient × divisor = dividend.

questions.q: Compute ¾ ÷ ⅖.
Compute 2½ ÷ 1¼.

days.guide: Ask how many ⅙ fit in ⅔ using fraction strips; then show a sample wrong answer (3/2 × ⅙ = ¼) and have the child critique it.

questions.q: Why is ⅔ ÷ ⅙ = 4?
questions.a: ⅔ = 4/6, so four ⅙-pieces fit in ⅔.

questions.q: A student wrote ⅔ ÷ ⅙ = 3/2 × ⅙ = ¼. What went wrong?
questions.a: They flipped the dividend instead of the divisor. Correct: ⅔ × 6/1 = 4.

days.guide: Give the quiz, including one written explanation.

questions.q: Compute 4 ÷ ⅔.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) ½ ÷ ⅛ = 4 2) ⅗ ÷ 3/10 = 2 3) ⅚ ÷ ⅔ = 5/4 = 1¼ 4) 4 ÷ ⅔ = 6 5) 1¾ ÷ ½ = 3½ 6) 2⅔ ÷ 1⅓ = 2 7) ⅞ ÷ 3 = 7/24 8) 9/10 ÷ ⅗ = 3/2 = 1½. Written explanation: 4 = diagram plus clear reasoning (e.g., ⅔ = 4/6, so four ⅙-pieces), 3 = correct with minor gaps, 2 = computation only, 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Gather: ribbon or string, ruler, recipe card. Mark a 4½-yard length of ribbon or string for Day 1 (a yardstick helps).
misconceptions: Writing the division backwards (⅜ ÷ 4½). Ask: 'What is being split up (the total), and what is the size of each piece?' Total goes first.
Rounding a 'how many pieces' answer up when partial pieces don't count.

days.guide: Measure ribbon to show the problem concretely, then compute 4½ ÷ ⅜. The child solves 6 similar problems.

questions.q: How many ⅜-yard pieces can be cut from 4½ yards?

days.guide: Review A = l × w, so w = A ÷ l. Model area 2½, width ¾.

questions.q: A rectangle has area 2½ sq ft and width ¾ ft. Find the length.

days.guide: Ask: 'If the recipe needs ⅔ cup and we only have a ½-cup scoop, how many scoops?' The child solves 5 recipe problems.

questions.q: How many ½-cup scoops make ⅔ cup?
questions.a: 1⅓ scoops.

days.guide: The child writes three fraction-division stories and an answer key; a family member solves them and the child checks.

questions.q: Solve: 5 cups of soup poured into ⅔-cup bowls. How many bowls?
questions.a: 7½ bowls (5 × 3/2).

days.guide: Give the word-problem quiz.

questions.q: Jo walked ¾ mile, which is ⅗ of her route. How long is the route?
questions.a: 1¼ miles.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 6 ÷ ¾ = 8 2) 3¾ ÷ ¼ = 15 3) ⅝ ÷ ¼ = 2½ 4) area 4½ sq ft, length 1½ ft → width 3 ft 5) 2¼ lb shared by 3 people → ¾ lb each 6) Jo walked ¾ mile, which is ⅗ of her route → route = ¾ ÷ ⅗ = 1¼ miles.

weeks.prep: Gather: small box, 1/2-inch cubes or sugar cubes, ruler. Choose a small box whose edges are whole or half inches. Sugar cubes are roughly ½ inch, so counts will be approximate.
misconceptions: Thinking a ½-inch cube has volume ½ cubic inch. It's ½ × ½ × ½ = ⅛ cubic inch; 8 fit in a 1-inch cube.
Confusing B (area of the base) with b (a base length).

days.guide: Pack the box with ½-inch cubes, counting rows × columns × layers. Show the count × ⅛ = l × w × h.

questions.q: A box is 2 in × 1½ in × 1 in. How many ½-inch cubes fill it, and what is its volume?
questions.a: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cubes; 24 × ⅛ = 3 cubic inches = 2 × 1½ × 1.

days.guide: Model V = lwh and V = Bh where B is the base area. The child computes the 10 volumes.

questions.q: Find the volume of a prism 2½ × 3 × 1½.
questions.a: 11¼ cubic units.

questions.q: A prism's base has area 10½ sq in and height 2 in. Volume?
questions.a: 21 cubic inches.

days.guide: Write V = l × w × h with a blank; multiply the known edges and divide.

questions.q: Volume 30 cu in, length 4 in, width 2½ in. Height?

days.guide: Assign the mixed review plus a garden-bed design: the child chooses dimensions and computes soil needed.

questions.q: A garden bed is 6 ft × 2½ ft × ¾ ft. How much soil fills it?
questions.a: 11¼ cubic feet.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test, then a short reflection on the two meanings of division.

questions.q: How many ½-inch cubes fill a 1-inch cube?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test sample key: 1) ¾ ÷ ⅜ = 2 2) 5 ÷ ⅚ = 6 3) 2⅓ ÷ ⅔ = 3½ 4) prism 2½ × 3 × 1½ → 11¼ cubic units 5) volume 30, l = 4, w = 2½ → h = 3 6) how many ½-in cubes fill a 2 × 1 × 1 in box? 16 7) 3½ yards cut into ½-yard pieces → 7 8) garden bed 6 × 2½ × ¾ ft → 11¼ cu ft. Reflection names 'how many groups' or 'how much in one group'.

weeks.prep: Gather: base-ten blocks or grid paper, receipts. Write a 4–5 item shopping list with prices for Day 1.
misconceptions: Lining up the last digits instead of the decimal points when adding. Write zeros as placeholders (4.5 → 4.50).
Placing the decimal in a product by lining it up. Count total decimal places in the factors (0.3 × 0.4 has 2 → 0.12).

days.guide: Write a shopping list with prices; stack decimals vertically on graph paper, then find change from $50.

questions.q: Items cost $12.49, $3.75 and $8.06. Total and change from $50?
questions.a: Total $24.30; change $25.70.

days.guide: Model 10.05 − 3.7 by writing 3.70 and regrouping. The child solves 20 problems.

questions.q: Compute 6 − 2.348.
Compute 10.05 − 3.7.

days.guide: Shade a 10 × 10 grid: 3 tenths one way, 4 tenths the other; overlap = 12 hundredths. Then teach counting decimal places.

questions.q: Compute 0.3 × 0.4 and explain the decimal placement.
Compute 0.07 × 0.5.

days.guide: Work the fabric problem; the child solves 5 similar ones and rounds money to the nearest cent.

questions.q: Fabric is $4.75 per yard. Cost of 2.5 yards?

days.guide: Give the decimal quiz.

questions.q: Compute 2.5 × 1.6.

weeks.prep: Gather: graph paper for aligning digits. Day 5 is the semester-1 review — glance back at the weeks 1–17 tests to see which skills need refreshing.
misconceptions: Forgetting to write a 0 in the quotient when a divisor doesn't go into a partial dividend.
Moving the decimal in the divisor but not the dividend. Both must be multiplied by the same power of 10.

days.guide: Model 864 ÷ 24 with partial quotients (24 × 30 = 720, remainder 144 = 24 × 6 → 36), then the standard algorithm side by side.

questions.q: Compute 864 ÷ 24.

days.guide: Practice divide–multiply–subtract–bring down, checking each by multiplying.

questions.q: Compute 7,392 ÷ 16.
Compute 1,035 ÷ 23.

days.guide: Show 4.56 ÷ 1.2 becomes 45.6 ÷ 12 by multiplying both by 10. The child solves 12 problems.

questions.q: Compute 7.2 ÷ 0.08.
Compute 4.56 ÷ 1.2.

days.guide: Work the bill problem together, then the child solves the rest and checks reasonableness by estimating.

questions.q: Split $47.85 equally among 3 people.
312.6 miles on 12 gallons — miles per gallon?

days.guide: Give the cumulative quiz; review weak areas next week.

questions.q: Compute 9.12 ÷ 0.24.

weeks.assessment_key: Semester 1 cumulative quiz key: 1) triangle b = 10, h = 7 → 35 2) boys:girls 3:5, 40 students → 15 boys, 25 girls 3) 30% of 90 = 27 4) 18 is 40% of 45 5) ¾ ÷ ⅛ = 6 6) 2⅖ ÷ ⅗ = 4 7) 6.3 × 0.4 = 2.52 8) 9.12 ÷ 0.24 = 38 9) $3.60 for 8 oz → $0.45/oz 10) prism 2 × 3 × 4: SA = 52 sq units, V = 24 cubic units.

weeks.prep: Gather: colored tiles, grid paper. Have colored square tiles or cut paper squares for the Day 1 tiling problem.
misconceptions: Mixing up GCF and LCM. GCF is the biggest number that divides both (splitting into equal groups); LCM is the smallest number both divide into (when things line up again).
Factoring out a common factor that isn't the greatest (36 + 8 = 2(18 + 4)). Correct but not fully factored — ask 'can the numbers in the parentheses still share a factor?'

days.guide: Draw a 24 × 36 rectangle. Try 4×4, 6×6 and 12×12 tiles; ask which is the largest that fits exactly with no gaps. Connect to listing factors of both numbers, then the child finds GCF for 10 pairs.

questions.q: What is the largest square tile that exactly covers a 24 × 36 rectangle, and how many tiles?
questions.a: 12 × 12 tiles; 2 × 3 = 6 tiles (GCF of 24 and 36 is 12).

questions.q: Find GCF(18, 30) and GCF(42, 56).
questions.a: 6 and 14.

days.guide: List multiples of 10 (10, 20, 30, 40…) and of 8 (8, 16, 24, 32, 40…) to find the first match. The child solves the hot-dog problems and 10 LCM pairs.

questions.q: Hot dogs come in packs of 10, buns in packs of 8. Fewest of each to have equal numbers?
questions.a: 40 of each: 4 packs of hot dogs, 5 packs of buns.

days.guide: Teach the cue: splitting into identical groups → GCF; events repeating and lining up → LCM. The child sorts and solves 8 problems.

questions.q: 24 pencils and 36 erasers go into identical kits with none left. Most kits?
questions.a: 12 kits (GCF), each with 2 pencils and 3 erasers.

questions.q: One bus comes every 12 minutes and another every 18. Both leave now; when together again?
questions.a: In 36 minutes (LCM).

days.guide: Draw a rectangle of area 36 + 8 split into two parts with a common height of 4 (4 × 9 and 4 × 2). Write 36 + 8 = 4(9 + 2) and have the child rewrite sums using the GCF.

questions.q: Rewrite 24 + 60 using the GCF.
Rewrite 36 + 8 using the GCF and check.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test independently and review errors together.

questions.q: GCF(48, 60) and LCM(6, 8)?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test sample key: 1) 4.7 + 12.38 = 17.08 2) 15.2 − 8.75 = 6.45 3) 2.4 × 0.35 = 0.84 4) 1,512 ÷ 24 = 63 5) 8.4 ÷ 0.07 = 120 6) GCF(48, 60) = 12 7) LCM(4, 6) = 12 8) LCM(6, 8) = 24 9) 45 + 30 = 15(3 + 2) 10) 18 cookies and 24 brownies on identical plates with nothing left over: at most 6 plates, each with 3 cookies and 4 brownies.

weeks.prep: Gather: index cards. Make index cards: 8 phrases, 8 matching expressions and 8 tape diagrams for the Day 3 game.
misconceptions: Reversing subtraction: '7 less than y' is y − 7, not 7 − y. Test with a number: 7 less than 10 is 3.
Reading 3x as 'three plus x'. 3x means 3 times x.

days.guide: Model translating with a real number first ('5 more than 3' → 3 + 5) then a variable. The child translates 15 phrases.

questions.q: Write expressions: 'x more than 5', 'a number divided by 3', '7 less than y'.

days.guide: Label the terms, coefficients and constants in 3x + 5y + 8 together; then the child labels 10 expressions.

questions.q: In 3x + 5y + 8, name the terms, coefficients and constant.
questions.a: Terms: 3x, 5y, 8. Coefficients: 3 and 5. Constant: 8.

questions.q: Describe 2(x + 5) in words.
questions.a: The product of 2 and the sum of x and 5.

days.guide: Play memory or matching with the cards. When a match is made, the child explains why it fits.

questions.q: Which matches 'add 1 to a number, then divide by 4': n/4 + 1 or (n + 1)/4?
questions.a: (n + 1)/4 — the parentheses show the adding happens first.

days.guide: Model substituting: replace the letter with the number in parentheses, then compute.

questions.q: Evaluate 3x + 4 when x = 2.5.
Evaluate 5(y − 2) when y = 6.

days.guide: Give the expression quiz.

questions.q: Write an expression for the cost of t tickets at $12 each plus a $5 fee.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 8 more than n → n + 8 2) the product of 6 and a number → 6n 3) a number divided by 5 → n/5 4) 3 less than twice x → 2x − 3 5) In 4x + 9: coefficient 4, constant 9, terms 4x and 9 6) 3x + 4 when x = 2.5 → 11.5 7) 10 − 2y when y = 3 → 4 8) (m + 6)/2 when m = 8 → 7 9) cost of t tickets at $12 plus a $5 fee → 12t + 5.

weeks.prep: Gather: balance scale or hanger diagram printouts, paper clips. Make a coat-hanger balance with two cups and paper clips, or print hanger diagrams.
misconceptions: Doing different operations to each side. Whatever you do to one side of the balance, you must do to the other.
Dividing the wrong way: for 3x = 12 some write x = 3/12. Ask 'what times 3 is 12?'

days.guide: Show that an equation is a statement that can be true or false; substitute values to test. The child tests 10 equations.

questions.q: Is x = 4 a solution to 3x + 2 = 14?
Is x = 5 a solution to x + 7 = 13?
questions.a: No: 5 + 7 = 12, not 13 (the solution is 6).

days.guide: Hang 3 clips plus a 'mystery bag' on one side and 7 clips on the other; remove 3 from each side. Draw the hanger diagram alongside.

questions.q: Solve x + 3 = 7 and 3x = 12 using the balance idea.
questions.a: x = 4 (remove 3 from both sides); x = 4 (split both sides into 3 equal groups).

days.guide: Model subtracting the same amount from both sides, then substituting to check. The child solves 12 problems.

questions.q: Solve x + 2.7 = 5.
Solve x + ¾ = 2½.
questions.a: x = 1¾.

days.guide: Model dividing both sides by the coefficient (or multiplying by its reciprocal). The child solves 12 and writes stories for two.

questions.q: Solve ⅔x = 10.
questions.a: x = 15 (multiply both sides by 3/2).

questions.q: Solve 4x = 9.2.

days.guide: Give the quiz; the child must write the equation before solving each word problem.

questions.q: 5 notebooks cost $13.75. Write and solve an equation for the price of one.

weeks.prep: Gather: algebra tiles (paper). Cut paper algebra tiles: long rectangles for x, small squares for 1.
misconceptions: Distributing only to the first term: 3(x + 2) = 3x + 2. Draw the area model to show 3 is multiplied by both x and 2.
Combining unlike terms (2x + 5 = 7x). Only like terms (same variable part) combine.

days.guide: Make a table with x = 0, 1, 5, 10 and evaluate both 3(x + 2) and 3x + 6. Then try 3(x + 2) vs 3x + 2.

questions.q: Are 3(x + 2) and 3x + 2 equivalent?
questions.a: No — at x = 0 they give 6 and 2.

questions.q: Values of 3(x + 2) and 3x + 6 at x = 5?
questions.a: Both 21.

days.guide: Draw a rectangle 4 tall and (x + 3) wide, split into 4·x and 4·3. Reverse it for factoring.

questions.q: Expand 4(x + 3) and 5(2y − 1).
Factor 6x + 18.

days.guide: Lay out 2 x-tiles + 5 unit tiles + 3 x-tiles + 1 unit tile; group like tiles.

questions.q: Simplify 2x + 5 + 3x + 1.
Why is x + x equal to 2x, not x²?
questions.a: Two of the same unknown amount added is 2 times x; x² would be x multiplied by x.

days.guide: For each pair, the child either names a property (distributive, commutative) or finds a value that gives different results.

questions.q: Is 2(x + 4) equivalent to 2x + 4? Justify.
questions.a: No. Counterexample x = 1: 2(5) = 10 but 2 + 4 = 6.

questions.q: Is x · x equivalent to 2x?
questions.a: No: x = 3 gives 9 and 6.

days.guide: Give the quiz independently.

questions.q: Factor 9a + 6.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 4(x + 3) = 4x + 12 2) 7(2 + y) = 14 + 7y 3) 12x + 20 = 4(3x + 5) 4) 9a + 6 = 3(3a + 2) 5) 3x + 4 + 5x − 1 = 8x + 3 6) 2(x + 4) and 2x + 8: equivalent 7) 5x − x and 5: not equivalent (x = 2 gives 8 and 5) 8) 6(x + 1) and 6x + 1: not equivalent (x = 0 gives 6 and 1).

weeks.prep: Gather: sheet of paper for folding, calculator. Have a sheet of paper for folding and a calculator for checking.
misconceptions: Thinking 2⁵ means 2 × 5. It means 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.
Working strictly left to right. Order: parentheses, exponents, multiply/divide left to right, add/subtract left to right.

days.guide: Fold the paper in half and count layers after each fold; record 2, 4, 8… as powers of 2. Ask the child to predict 10 folds.

questions.q: How many layers after 10 folds?
questions.a: 2¹⁰ = 1,024 layers.

days.guide: Write 3⁴ as 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 before computing. The child evaluates 15 expressions.

questions.q: Evaluate 3⁴, (½)³ and 0.2².
Which is larger, 2⁵ or 5²?
questions.a: 2⁵ = 32 is larger than 5² = 25.

days.guide: Model 2 + 3 × 4² step by step, then (2 + 3)². The child finds the errors in three worked examples.

questions.q: Evaluate 2 + 3 × 4².
Evaluate (2 + 3)².

days.guide: Substitute into formulas, writing the formula, the substitution, then the answer.

questions.q: A cube box has edge 1.5 ft. Find its volume and surface area.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: Evaluate 4 + 2³ × 5.

weeks.prep: Gather: graph paper, Desmos. Have a kitchen scale and a cup for the Day 3 water experiment.
misconceptions: Swapping independent and dependent variables. Ask: 'Which one do I choose or control? That's independent (x-axis).'
Thinking every relationship's graph starts at (0,0). y = x + 3 starts at (0,3).

days.guide: Ask: 'If you earn $9 per hour, what decides how much you earn?' Name hours as independent, dollars as dependent, and write d = 9h.

questions.q: For $9 per hour, write an equation and find earnings for 6 hours.
Which variable is independent?
questions.a: Hours worked (h); pay depends on it.

days.guide: Make tables for x = 0–5 for each equation and plot all three on one grid. Compare: which go through (0,0), which is steepest?

questions.q: At x = 2, find y for y = 4x, y = x + 3 and y = 2.5x.
Which graph does not pass through the origin?
questions.a: y = x + 3 (it starts at 3).

days.guide: Weigh the empty cup, then add 2 tablespoons at a time and weigh. Make a table and graph; help write an equation like w = (cup weight) + 15t (1 tbsp of water ≈ 15 g).

questions.q: If the cup weighs 150 g and each tablespoon of water adds about 15 g, what is the weight after 6 tablespoons?

days.guide: Assign the mixed review; check equations and graphs for labels.

questions.q: Solve x + 4.5 = 10 and ⅗x = 9.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test; the child corrects errors.

questions.q: Evaluate 2³ + 4 × 3.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test sample key: 1) 'x decreased by 7' → x − 7 2) 4a + 3 when a = 1.5 → 9 3) x + 4.5 = 10 → x = 5.5 4) (3/5)x = 9 → x = 15 5) 3(2x + 5) = 6x + 15 6) factor 8x + 12 = 4(2x + 3) 7) 2³ + 4 × 3 = 20 8) A train goes 60 mph: d = 60t; at t = 3.5, d = 210 miles 9) In d = 60t, t is independent and d dependent 10) 6x + 2 + x = 7x + 2.

weeks.prep: Gather: outdoor thermometer, number line strip. Check today's temperature on an outdoor thermometer; make a −10 to 10 number-line strip.
misconceptions: Thinking −5 is greater than −2 because 5 > 2. On the number line, −5 is farther left, so it is less.
Thinking zero always means 'nothing'. In elevation, 0 is sea level; in temperature, 0° is just a point on the scale.

days.guide: Discuss California extremes: Badwater Basin in Death Valley is 282 ft below sea level (−282), Mount Whitney is about 14,505 ft above. Ask what 0 means for elevation and temperature.

questions.q: What does an elevation of −282 feet mean?
questions.a: 282 feet below sea level (0 = sea level).

days.guide: Mark pairs like 3 and −3 at equal distances from 0. Explain −(−4) as 'the opposite of the opposite of 4'.

questions.q: What is the opposite of −2.5? Of ¾?
questions.a: 2.5 and −¾.

questions.q: Why does −(−4) = 4?
questions.a: −4 is the opposite of 4; the opposite of that is back to 4.

days.guide: Model a deposit as +, a withdrawal or debt as −. The child writes signed numbers for 8 situations.

questions.q: Write signed numbers: deposit $50; withdraw $20; owe $15.

days.guide: Draw −3 to 3 with tick marks every ½ or ¼. The child places −2.5, −¾, 1.25, 2⅓ etc.

questions.q: Between which two integers is −¾? Is it closer to 0 or −1?
questions.a: Between −1 and 0, closer to −1.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: Which is colder: −5°F or −12°F?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 20 ft below sea level → −20 ft 2) a gain of 7 yards → +7 3) opposite of −8 → 8 4) −(−6) = 6 5) a bank balance of 0 means you have no money and owe nothing 6) −1.5 halfway between −2 and −1; ¾ between 0 and 1; −2⅓ just left of −2 7) −12°F is colder than −5°F.

weeks.prep: Gather: index cards with rational numbers. Write about 12 rational numbers (integers, fractions, decimals, positive and negative) on index cards.
misconceptions: Ordering negatives by their size without the sign (−1.5 < −2). Use the number line: farther left is less.
Thinking absolute value 'just makes things positive' without meaning. Stress it is distance from 0.

days.guide: Place −7 and −3 on the number line and model reading '−7 < −3' as '−7 is to the left of −3'.

questions.q: Compare −7 and −3 with < or >.

days.guide: Shuffle the cards; the child orders them on the table, converting fractions to decimals when unsure.

questions.q: Order 0.3, −2.5, 3/2, −½, 1 from least to greatest.

days.guide: Show |−8| as 8 steps from 0. Connect to debt: balance −30 means a debt of |−30| = $30.

questions.q: Find |−8| and |3.5|.
An account balance is −30 dollars. What is the size of the debt?

days.guide: Contrast 'which is less?' with 'which is farther from 0?' in contexts like debts and depths.

questions.q: Is −24 < −14? Is |−24| > |−14|? Explain with debt.
questions.a: Both true: a balance of −24 is lower, and a debt of $24 is larger than a debt of $14.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: True or false: |−9| < |4|.
questions.a: False; 9 > 4.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) −7 < −3 2) −1.5 > −2 3) order {2, −3.5, −¼, 0, −1} → −3.5, −1, −¼, 0, 2 4) |−12| = 12 5) |5| = 5 6) balances −40 and −25: −40 is the greater debt ($40) 7) |−9| < |4| is false (9 > 4) 8) −120 m is farther below sea level than −86 m.

weeks.prep: Gather: number line strips. Make number-line strips the child can draw on.
misconceptions: Using an open circle for ≥ or ≤. Closed (filled) circle means the number itself is included.
Reading 'at least' as <. 'At least 48' means 48 or more: h ≥ 48.

days.guide: Translate key phrases: at least (≥), at most/no more than (≤), more than (>), fewer than (<). The child writes 10.

questions.q: Write inequalities: at least 48 inches to ride; fewer than 30 students.

days.guide: Graph x > 3 (open circle at 3, shade right) and x ≤ −1 (closed at −1, shade left). The child tests values by substitution.

questions.q: Describe the graph of x ≤ −1.
questions.a: A closed circle at −1 with shading to the left.

days.guide: Ask the child to name solutions of x > 3 that get closer and closer to 3 (3.1, 3.01, 3.001). Discuss why there are infinitely many.

questions.q: Is 3 a solution of x > 3? Is 3.001?
questions.a: 3 is not; 3.001 is.

questions.q: Why does x > 3 have infinitely many solutions?
questions.a: Every number greater than 3, including all decimals and fractions, makes it true.

days.guide: Discuss when only whole numbers make sense (people) vs decimals (money).

questions.q: A van holds at most 7 people. Write an inequality and list solutions that make sense.
questions.a: p ≤ 7; p = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 or 7 (whole numbers only).

questions.q: You need to save at least $120. Write an inequality.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: Write: no more than $20.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) at least 48 inches → h ≥ 48 2) fewer than 30 students → s < 30 3) no more than $20 → c ≤ 20 4) more than 5 → x > 5 5) x < −2: open circle at −2, shaded left 6) Is 4 a solution of x ≥ 4? Yes 7) Is −1 a solution of x > 0? No 8) An elevator holds at most 1,500 lb → w ≤ 1,500.

weeks.prep: Gather: graph paper, Desmos. Draw a large four-quadrant grid; plan a simple neighborhood map for Day 4.
misconceptions: Plotting (x, y) as (y, x). Remind: 'walk before you climb' — x is horizontal first.
Counting tick marks instead of spaces when finding distance.

days.guide: Review quadrant numbering (I top-right, counterclockwise). The child plots 20 points and names quadrants.

questions.q: Name the quadrant of (−3, 4), (2, −5) and (−1.5, −2).
questions.a: II, IV and III.

days.guide: Plot (3, −2) and its reflections over each axis. Ask which coordinate changed sign.

questions.q: Reflect (3, −2) over the x-axis and over the y-axis.
questions.a: (3, 2) and (−3, −2). Over the x-axis the y-sign flips; over the y-axis the x-sign flips.

days.guide: For points sharing a y-coordinate, subtract x-values or add absolute values when on opposite sides of 0.

questions.q: Distance from (−3, 4) to (5, 4)?
Distance from (2, −6) to (2, 3)?
questions.a: 9 units.

days.guide: Place home at (0,0), each block = 1 unit. The child marks 5 places and finds street distances (only horizontal and vertical moves).

questions.q: School is at (4, −3). How many blocks does the child walk along streets from home?
questions.a: 7 blocks (4 east + 3 south).

days.guide: Give the quiz and collect the map.

questions.q: Reflect (−6, 1) over the y-axis.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) (−4, 2) Quadrant II 2) (5, −1) Quadrant IV 3) (−2.5, −3) Quadrant III 4) (−6, 1) reflected over the x-axis → (−6, −1) 5) reflected over the y-axis → (6, 1) 6) distance from (−3, 4) to (5, 4) = 8 7) (1, −7) to (1, 2) = 9 8) (−5, −2) to (−5, −9) = 7. Map project rubric: 4 = home at origin, at least 5 labeled places, correct coordinates and street distances; 3 = minor errors; 2 = several errors; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: graph paper, Desmos. Graph paper; optionally set up Desmos for the Day 4 design.
misconceptions: Finding side length by subtracting a negative incorrectly (4 − (−3) = 1). Count on the grid or use |4| + |−3| = 7.
Using perimeter when area is asked.

days.guide: Give vertex lists; the child plots and connects in order. Check that rectangles have square corners.

questions.a: A rectangle 7 units wide and 3 tall.

days.guide: Find horizontal and vertical side lengths using coordinates, then perimeters.

questions.q: Find the perimeter of that rectangle.

days.guide: Decompose or enclose in a rectangle and subtract corner triangles.

questions.q: Area of the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (6, 0), (2, 4)?
questions.a: 12 square units (½ × 6 × 4).

questions.q: Area of the rectangle from Day 1?
questions.a: 21 square units.

days.guide: Challenge the child to design a garden with area exactly 48. Rectangles are fine; encourage an L-shape for extra challenge.

questions.q: Give rectangle vertices with area 48.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test.

questions.q: Distance from (−2, 5) to (−2, −3)?
questions.a: 8 units.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test sample key: 1) −3 < −1.5 2) order −2, −⅓, 0.5, 1¼ 3) |−15| = 15 4) at least 12 → x ≥ 12 5) x < 4: open circle at 4, shade left 6) (−2, 5) Quadrant II 7) distance (−2, 5) to (−2, −3) = 8 8) rectangle (−3, 2), (4, 2), (4, −1), (−3, −1): perimeter 20, area 21 9) (4, −3) reflected over the y-axis → (−4, −3) 10) −8°F is colder than −3°F.

weeks.prep: Gather: family survey sheet, graph paper. Write the survey question with your child before Day 2 and line up 20+ people to ask (family, friends, co-op, by phone).
misconceptions: Thinking any question with a number answer is statistical. It must expect variability across many answers.
Spacing dot-plot values unevenly or skipping values with no data. The number line must be evenly scaled.

days.guide: Contrast 'How old am I?' (one answer) with 'How old are students at my co-op?' (many varying answers). The child sorts 12 and writes 3.

questions.q: Is 'How many pets does each family on our street have?' statistical?
questions.a: Yes — answers vary from family to family.

days.guide: The child surveys 20+ people and tallies a frequency table.

questions.q: Why survey at least 20 people?
questions.a: More data gives a clearer picture of the variability and typical values.

days.guide: Model a dot plot: an evenly scaled number line with one dot per response stacked above its value.

questions.q: In a dot plot of screen time, a stack of 5 dots above 2 means what?
questions.a: Five people reported 2 hours of screen time.

days.guide: Teach the vocabulary: center (typical value), spread (how far values range), shape (symmetric, skewed, clusters, gaps, outliers).

questions.a: Center about 3; most values between 1 and 5; 9 is an outlier; skewed right.

days.guide: Give the quiz and collect the survey dot plot.

questions.q: Rewrite 'What is my favorite food?' as a statistical question.
questions.a: Example: 'What are the favorite foods of the people in my family?' (or any question expecting varied answers).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) 'How tall is the Eiffel Tower?' — not statistical (one answer) 2) 'How many hours do 6th graders sleep on school nights?' — statistical 3) For data 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 9: center about 3, most values from 1 to 5, 9 is an outlier, shape skewed right. Survey dot-plot rubric: 4 = statistical question, 20+ responses, frequency table, evenly scaled labeled dot plot, written description of center/spread/shape; 3 = one element weak; 2 = two missing; 1 = mostly incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: stopwatch, graph paper. Practice the ruler-drop test: one person holds a 30 cm ruler at 0; the child catches it and you read the cm mark.
misconceptions: Unequal bin widths or gaps between bars. Bins must be equal width, and bars touch.
Reading a histogram bar as one data value. Each bar shows how many values fall in a range.

days.guide: Do 25 ruler drops and record catch distances in cm (smaller = faster reaction).

questions.q: If the catch distance is smaller, is the reaction faster or slower?
questions.a: Faster — the ruler fell a shorter distance before being caught.

days.guide: Choose a bin width (e.g., 3 cm), tally the data in bins and draw touching bars.

questions.q: Why do histogram bars touch?
questions.a: The bins are continuous ranges of numbers with no gaps between them.

days.guide: Draw a dot plot and histogram of the same data; discuss what each shows.

questions.q: When is a histogram better than a dot plot?
questions.a: With many data values or a wide range, where grouping shows the shape more clearly.

days.guide: Use the dog-weight histogram in the key (and a temperature one). The child answers questions and describes shape.

questions.q: Using the dog histogram (4, 7, 5, 2, 1 dogs in 20-lb bins from 0), how many dogs weigh 40 lb or more?

days.guide: Give the quiz and collect the reaction-time display.

questions.q: Can you find the exact heaviest dog's weight from the histogram?
questions.a: No — only that it is between 80 and 100 lb.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (dog-weight histogram, bins in lb: 0–20: 4, 20–40: 7, 40–60: 5, 60–80: 2, 80–100: 1): 1) total dogs = 19 2) most common bin 20–40 lb 3) dogs 40 lb or more = 8 4) shape skewed right 5) you cannot tell the exact heaviest weight, only that it is 80–100 lb. Display rubric: 4 = equal bins, labeled axes and title, accurate heights; 3 = one labeling error; 2 = unequal bins; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: snap cubes, ruler and pencil for balance. Have 20–30 snap cubes; a ruler balanced on a pencil helps show 'balance point'.
misconceptions: Forgetting to use absolute values for MAD, so deviations cancel to 0.
Thinking the mean must be one of the data values.

days.guide: Build towers of 3, 5, 7 and 9 cubes; move cubes until all are equal. Connect to adding (24) and dividing by 4.

questions.q: Towers of 3, 5, 7 and 9 cubes are leveled. How tall is each?

days.guide: Plot 2, 4, 6, 8 and mark the mean 5. Show distances below (3 + 1) equal distances above (1 + 3).

questions.q: Show that 5 is the balance point of 2, 4, 6, 8.
questions.a: Distances below: 3 + 1 = 4; above: 1 + 3 = 4. They balance.

days.guide: Model MAD: find the mean, find each distance from it, average the distances.

questions.q: Player A scored 10, 12, 14, 16, 18; Player B scored 6, 10, 14, 18, 22. Find each MAD. Who is more consistent?
questions.a: Both means are 14. A's MAD = 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4; B's = 24 ÷ 5 = 4.8. A is more consistent.

days.guide: Give two data sets: fertilized plants 12, 14, 15, 16, 18 cm and unfertilized 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 cm.

questions.q: Compare the groups using mean and MAD.
questions.a: Fertilized mean 15, MAD 1.6; unfertilized mean 11, MAD 1.2. Fertilized plants were about 4 cm taller on average; both groups had small variability.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: The mean of five numbers is 8; four are 6, 7, 9, 10. Find the fifth.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) mean of 4, 7, 9, 10, 15 = 9 2) MAD = (5 + 2 + 0 + 1 + 6) ÷ 5 = 2.8 3) 3, 3, 6, 8: mean 5, MAD = (2 + 2 + 1 + 3) ÷ 4 = 2 4) a team with MAD 1.5 is more consistent than one with MAD 3.2 5) mean of five numbers is 8 and four are 6, 7, 9, 10 → fifth is 8.

weeks.prep: Gather: index cards, graph paper. Write 11 data values on index cards (include one large outlier).
misconceptions: Finding the median without ordering data first.
Thinking each section of a box plot has the same number of values because sections are different lengths — each quarter holds about 25% of the data regardless of length.

days.guide: Order the 11 cards; the middle (6th) card is the median. Compare with the mean.

questions.q: Data: 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 40. Find the median and mean.
questions.a: Median 6; mean 98 ÷ 11 ≈ 8.9. The outlier 40 pulls the mean up but not the median.

days.guide: Split the ordered data at the median, find the median of each half (Q1, Q3).

questions.q: Five-number summary of 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12?
questions.a: Min 1, Q1 3.5, median 6.5, Q3 9, max 12; range 11, IQR 5.5.

days.guide: Draw a scaled number line, mark the five numbers, draw the box from Q1 to Q3 with a line at the median, then whiskers.

questions.q: What does the box in a box plot show?
questions.a: The middle 50% of the data, from Q1 to Q3.

days.guide: Give two box plots (e.g., City A: 55, 58, 62, 66, 70; City B: 60, 66, 72, 78, 84 for monthly highs °F). The child writes 3 conclusions.

questions.q: Which city is warmer typically and which varies more?
questions.a: City B: median 72 vs 62; IQR 12 vs 8 and range 24 vs 15, so B also varies more.

days.guide: Give the box-plot quiz.

questions.q: Find the IQR of 4, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 21.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: data 4, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 21 → min 4, Q1 7, median 10, Q3 15, max 21, range 17, IQR 8. Box plot drawn with box from 7 to 15, line at 10, whiskers to 4 and 21. For two box plots, the one with the higher median has the larger typical value; the one with the longer box has more variability in the middle half.

weeks.prep: Gather: survey or measurement tools, poster board or slides. Help the child choose a doable project question (e.g., 'How long do family members sleep?') and tools to collect 30 data points.
misconceptions: Using mean/MAD for strongly skewed data or data with outliers; median/IQR is better there.
Collecting too little data or a biased sample (only asking siblings).

days.guide: Show a symmetric set and a skewed set with an outlier; decide which measures fit each.

questions.q: House prices in a neighborhood include one mansion. Mean or median?
questions.a: Median (and IQR), because the outlier pulls the mean.

days.guide: The child writes the question, plans 30+ data points and starts collecting.

questions.q: Is 'What is my dog's weight?' a good project question?
questions.a: No — one answer, no variability. Better: 'What do dogs at the park weigh?'

days.guide: The child makes two displays and computes center and spread.

questions.q: Which two displays fit 30 measurements well?
questions.a: A dot plot or histogram plus a box plot.

days.guide: The child builds a poster or slides and presents; ask follow-up questions.

questions.q: What should the conclusion include?
questions.a: An answer to the question using a center and spread value, and a note about shape or outliers.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test.

questions.q: Mean and MAD of 2, 4, 4, 5, 10?
questions.a: Mean 5; MAD 2.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test sample key: 1) 'How many books did each student read this summer?' is statistical 2) mean of 2, 4, 4, 5, 10 = 5 3) MAD = (3 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 5) ÷ 5 = 2 4) median = 4 5) 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 12 → min 1, Q1 3, median 6, Q3 8.5, max 12, IQR 5.5 6) for skewed data use the median. Project rubric: 4 = statistical question, 30+ data points, two correct displays, correct center and spread, a conclusion that answers the question; 3 = minor calculation errors; 2 = one display or measure missing; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: map of California, online prices, spreadsheet or paper. Let the child pick a California destination and look up the driving distance and prices together.
misconceptions: Forgetting the return trip when computing fuel.
Adding tax as 8 instead of 8% (0.08 × total).

days.guide: Find distance and mpg; compute gallons and fuel cost.

questions.q: A 380-mile trip in a car getting 28 mpg needs how much gas? At $4.80/gal, cost?
questions.a: About 13.6 gallons; about $65.14 (one way).

days.guide: Build a budget table; add 8% tax by multiplying by 0.08 (or the total by 1.08).

questions.q: A $412.50 budget plus 8% tax?

days.guide: Use average speed to estimate driving time and plan stops.

questions.q: 380 miles at 60 mph takes how long?
questions.a: 6⅓ hours = 6 hours 20 minutes.

days.guide: Measure bags; compute volumes and compare with the trunk.

questions.q: A trunk holds 14 cu ft. Do four 2 × 1½ × ¾ ft suitcases fit by volume?
questions.a: Each is 2.25 cu ft; four = 9 cu ft, so yes by volume (shape matters too).

days.guide: The child presents the plan and answers questions.

questions.q: How would doubling the trip distance change fuel cost?
questions.a: It would double (fuel is proportional to distance).

weeks.assessment_key: Project rubric: 4 = all calculations correct and shown (fuel = distance ÷ mpg, cost, budget with 8% tax, time = distance ÷ speed, volume comparison), clear tables, confident explanation; 3 = one or two calculation errors; 2 = several sections incomplete; 1 = little math shown. Sample check: 380 mi at 28 mpg ≈ 13.6 gal; at $4.80/gal ≈ $65.14 one way; $412.50 budget + 8% tax = $445.50; 380 mi at 60 mph ≈ 6 h 20 min.

weeks.prep: Gather: review packets, Khan Academy course challenge. Print review sets; set up the Khan Academy 6th grade course challenge.
misconceptions: Rushing review — have the child star problems they are unsure of and revisit them.
Rounding too early in multi-step problems.

days.guide: The child works the ratio/number review set, starring uncertain problems; review starred ones together.

questions.q: Find 40% of 65 and compute 2½ ÷ ⅚.
questions.a: 26 and 3.

days.guide: The child works the expressions/geometry review set; review stars.

questions.q: Solve ⅔x = 18. Find the volume of a 2 × 3 × 4.5 prism.
questions.a: x = 27; 27 cubic units.

days.guide: The child works the rational numbers/data set, then takes the Khan Academy course challenge.

questions.q: Distance from (−4, 3) to (6, 3)? Median of 3, 9, 4, 7, 12, 5?
questions.a: 10 units; 6.

days.guide: Give the 40-problem final in one or two sittings without help.

questions.q: Evaluate 5 + 2 × 3².

days.guide: Correct the final together; the child writes a reflection and 2–3 goals for Math 7.

questions.q: Which topic grew most this year and what's a goal for next year?
questions.a: Answers vary; a strong reflection names a specific skill with evidence (e.g., 'I can now divide fractions using reciprocals') and a concrete goal.

PE.overview: Plan about 30–45 minutes of activity per lesson: warm up, teach one skill with 2–3 simple cues, practice it in drills, then apply it in a game, and end with a cool-down and a quick check question. Fitness tests (FitnessGram-style) happen at the start, middle and end of the year — compare your child only with their own earlier scores. Prioritize safety (clear space, water, proper shoes, heat awareness) and praise effort, teamwork and sportsmanship as much as skill.

weeks.prep: Gather: stopwatch, cones, water bottle. Clear a safe open space and set up cones. Know the signs of heat illness (dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps) and stop activity if they appear. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Holding static stretches before activity. Warm up with movement (dynamic) first; save held stretches for the cool-down.
Pressing too hard with the thumb to find a pulse. Use the index and middle fingers lightly.

days.guide: Model each of the 10 warm-up moves with a cue ('knees to hip height'); the child copies, then do the cool-down stretches, holding each 15–30 seconds.

questions.q: Why do a dynamic warm-up before exercise?
questions.a: It raises heart rate and muscle temperature and loosens joints, which helps prevent injury.

days.guide: Show the radial (thumb side of the wrist) and carotid (side of the neck) pulses. The child counts for 15 seconds and multiplies by 4.

questions.q: You count 19 beats in 15 seconds. What is your heart rate?
questions.a: 76 beats per minute.

days.guide: Walk, jog and sprint 1 minute each, measuring pulse right after; graph.

questions.q: Which activity should produce the highest heart rate, and why?
questions.a: Sprinting — higher intensity means muscles need more oxygen, so the heart pumps faster.

days.guide: Play tag, then discuss heat safety, hydration and shoes; the child sets a water goal.

questions.q: Name two signs of heat illness and what to do.
questions.a: Dizziness, headache, nausea, cramps, heavy sweating or confusion; stop, move to shade, drink water and tell an adult.

days.guide: The child leads the warm-up; give the quiz.

questions.q: Where do you find the carotid pulse?
questions.a: On the side of the neck, beside the windpipe.

weeks.assessment_key: Student-led warm-up checklist (4 = leads all 10 moves in order with correct form cues and counts, explains warm-up purpose; 3 = minor omissions; 2 = needs prompting; 1 = can't lead). Heart-rate log: resting rate (typically about 60–100 bpm for this age), plus walk/jog/sprint rates rising in order. Quiz: 1) warm-ups raise heart rate and body temperature and prepare muscles to prevent injury 2) count beats for 15 seconds × 4 = beats per minute 3) radial pulse at the wrist, carotid at the neck 4) heart rate rises with intensity.

weeks.prep: Gather: PACER audio (free online) or measured 20 m course, mat, measuring tape. Download the free PACER audio or measure a 20 m course (or a 1-mile route). Use a mat for curl-ups. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Starting the PACER or mile too fast. Pace steadily.
Curl-ups with hands behind the head pulling the neck. Arms stay straight, fingers slide along the mat strip.

days.guide: Explain the PACER: run 20 m before the beep; the beeps speed up; the test ends at the second missed beep. Or time a mile run/walk.

questions.q: When does the PACER end?
questions.a: When you fail to reach the line before the beep for the second time.

days.guide: Teach curl-up form: knees bent about 140°, feet flat, arms straight, fingertips slide across a measuring strip, one curl every 3 seconds.

questions.q: Name two correct curl-up form cues.
questions.a: Arms straight with palms sliding on the mat; head returns to the mat each rep; feet flat; keep the 3-second cadence.

days.guide: Teach push-up form: straight body, lower until elbows are at 90°, one every 3 seconds.

questions.q: What counts as a correct push-up in the FitnessGram test?
questions.a: Body straight from head to heels, lowering until the elbows bend to 90° and pushing back up, in rhythm.

days.guide: Play frisbee catch lightly; record scores in the log.

questions.q: Why include an easy recovery day after testing?
questions.a: Muscles recover and rebuild; light activity reduces soreness.

days.guide: Compare results with HFZ charts for age and sex.

questions.q: What does 'Healthy Fitness Zone' mean?
questions.a: A score range linked to good health for your age and sex — the goal, not a competition.

weeks.assessment_key: Baseline log: PACER laps or mile time, curl-ups and push-ups (all reps at the 3-second cadence with correct form). Scored for completeness and accurate counting; results compared to FitnessGram Healthy Fitness Zone (HFZ) charts on Day 5.

weeks.prep: Gather: box and ruler for sit-and-reach, fitness log. Build a sit-and-reach box (or use a box and yardstick). Have the fitness log. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Bouncing in the sit-and-reach. Reach slowly and hold.
Arching the back hard and fast in the trunk lift. Lift slowly; the test stops at 12 inches.

days.guide: Back-saver sit-and-reach: one leg straight, other knee bent; reach four times, hold the fourth; both sides.

questions.q: Why test one leg at a time?
questions.a: It protects the lower back and checks each hamstring separately.

days.guide: Trunk lift: lie face down, lift chest slowly, hold, measure chin height (max 12 inches). Teach supermans and bird-dogs.

questions.q: What does the trunk lift measure?
questions.a: Strength and flexibility of the back (trunk extensor) muscles.

days.guide: Teach the five components; match tests; play a circuit.

questions.q: Name the five components of health-related fitness.
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition.

questions.q: Which component does the PACER test?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory (aerobic) endurance.

days.guide: The child writes two SMART goals.

questions.q: Make this SMART: 'I want to run better.'
questions.a: Example: 'I will improve my PACER score from 20 to 28 laps by January by jogging 20 minutes three times a week.'

days.guide: Share goals; do a 20-minute goal circuit.

questions.q: What does the 'T' in SMART stand for?
questions.a: Time-bound — there is a deadline.

weeks.assessment_key: SMART goal rubric — 4: two goals that are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant (tied to a test below or near HFZ) and Time-bound, with a plan (e.g., 'I will increase my push-ups from 8 to 12 by the mid-year test by doing push-ups 3 days a week'); 3: one element missing; 2: vague; 1: none.

weeks.prep: Gather: blindfold, cones, hula hoop, rope. Set up a cone maze; use a soft blindfold; stay with the blindfolded child at all times. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Giving vague directions ('go there'). Use specific words: 'three small steps forward, turn left.'
Blaming teammates. Focus on solutions.

days.guide: Model precise directions; switch roles.

questions.q: What makes verbal directions effective?
questions.a: They are specific (distance, direction, number of steps), calm and checked for understanding.

days.guide: Pass the hoop around a hand-holding circle; time and improve.

questions.q: What strategy speeds the hoop pass?
questions.a: Plan movements together, step through rather than climb, and call out encouragement.

days.guide: Untangle a human knot.

questions.q: What communication strategy helps the knot?
questions.a: One person speaks at a time; describe moves before doing them; move slowly.

days.guide: Run the encouragement relay.

questions.q: Give an example of encouraging words.
questions.a: 'Nice effort!' 'You've got this!' 'Great try — keep going!'

days.guide: The child writes the reflection.

questions.q: Why does teamwork matter in physical activity?
questions.a: It helps groups solve problems, stay safe and enjoy activity together.

weeks.assessment_key: Teamwork self-assessment (1–4 on each): listened to others; gave clear directions; encouraged teammates; accepted feedback; plus written examples of one helpful action and one improvement.

weeks.prep: Gather: poly spots or paper plates, ball, rope. Gather poly spots or paper plates and soft balls. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Rushing in without planning. Plan for 2 minutes first.
Thinking modifications make games 'easier'. They make games fair and include everyone.

days.guide: Plan first, then cross the 'lava' using limited spots.

questions.q: Why plan before trying?
questions.a: Planning lets everyone understand roles and avoid repeated mistakes.

days.guide: Group juggle in a set pattern; add balls.

questions.q: What helps the group juggle?
questions.a: Saying the receiver's name before tossing and using gentle underhand tosses.

days.guide: Keep a balloon up, each person in order.

questions.q: What is a good strategy for keeping the balloon up?
questions.a: Gentle, high touches and calling the next person.

days.guide: Redesign a challenge for full inclusion.

questions.q: How could you adapt 'lava river' for a player who uses a wheelchair?
questions.a: Use larger spots or tape zones reachable by wheels, allow a partner to place spots, keep the path wide and flat.

days.guide: Record times and explain the best strategy.

questions.q: What should you do when a strategy fails?
questions.a: Talk as a group, identify the problem and try one change.

weeks.assessment_key: Strategy reflection rubric — 4: records best times, names the specific strategy change that helped most and explains why with data; 3: names a strategy without data; 2: vague; 1: missing.

weeks.prep: Gather: parachute or bedsheet, balls, pedometer or phone step counter. Use a bedsheet if no parachute; set up step counters. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Thinking cooperative games aren't real exercise. Track steps to show they can be vigorous.
Designing games where players sit out. Good games keep everyone moving.

days.guide: Play sheet games (popcorn, mushroom).

questions.q: Why does timing matter in sheet games?
questions.a: The sheet only lifts well when everyone moves together.

days.guide: Play cooperative tag; track steps.

questions.q: How does 'freeze tag with rescue' keep everyone active?
questions.a: Frozen players are freed by teammates instead of sitting out.

days.guide: Do a synced partner circuit.

questions.q: Why sync reps with a partner?
questions.a: It builds teamwork and keeps pace steady.

days.guide: Design and teach a cooperative game.

questions.q: What makes a game inclusive?
questions.a: Everyone participates, rules can be adapted, and no one is eliminated for long.

days.guide: Play and evaluate the game.

questions.q: How can you check a game's activity level?
questions.a: Count steps or heart rate during play.

weeks.assessment_key: Original game rubric — 4: clear written rules, safety rules, everyone active (no elimination or quick re-entry), inclusive modifications, successfully taught; 3: minor gaps; 2: unclear rules; 1: incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: soccer ball, cones. Set up a cone course and a 1 m cone gate. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Kicking with the toe. Pass with the inside of the foot.
Looking only at the ball. Look up between touches.

days.guide: Dribble the course with small touches.

questions.q: Name three parts of the foot used to dribble.
questions.a: Inside, outside and sole.

days.guide: Pass inside-foot at 5 and 10 m.

questions.q: Cues for an inside-foot pass?
questions.a: Plant foot beside the ball pointing at the target, ankle locked, strike with the inside of the foot, follow through.

days.guide: Trap with inside foot and thigh, then pass.

questions.q: How do you 'cushion' a ball when receiving?
questions.a: Give with the foot or thigh as the ball arrives to absorb its speed.

days.guide: Play 2v1 keep-away.

questions.q: Where should the receiver move?
questions.a: Into open space away from the defender, creating a passing lane.

days.guide: Run the skill check.

questions.q: Why keep the ball close when dribbling?
questions.a: So you keep control and defenders can't steal it.

weeks.assessment_key: Skill check: 10 inside-foot passes through a 1 m gate (score successes; 7+ = proficient) and a timed dribble course with close control (ball within about 1 m) using inside, outside and sole touches.

weeks.prep: Gather: soccer ball, goal or cones. Use a goal or two cones 3 m apart. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Leaning back on shots, sending the ball high. Keep head and knee over the ball.
Diving in on defense. Stay goal-side and jockey.

days.guide: Shoot instep at corners from 10 m.

questions.q: What part of the foot is used for a power shot?
questions.a: The instep (laces).

days.guide: 3v1 passing triangles.

questions.q: Why form triangles on offense?
questions.a: They create two passing options for the player with the ball.

days.guide: Defensive stance and jockeying.

questions.q: What does 'goal-side' mean?
questions.a: Staying between your opponent and your own goal.

days.guide: Small-sided game, rotating positions.

questions.q: What is fair play?
questions.a: Following rules, respecting opponents and officials, helping someone who falls.

days.guide: Write the reflection.

questions.q: Name an offensive strategy.
questions.a: Spreading out, passing triangles, moving to open space.

weeks.assessment_key: Game-play observation checklist (yes/no each): moves to open space; passes to open teammates; shoots with instep; stays goal-side on defense; jockeys rather than lunging; plays fair and encourages. Reflection names one offensive and one defensive strategy with an example.

weeks.prep: Gather: flying disc, cones. Use a soft flying disc; cones for targets. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Throwing with an angled release. Keep the disc flat.
Catching with one hand while learning. Use two hands (pancake).

days.guide: Practice backhand.

questions.q: What causes a disc to curve or dive?
questions.a: Releasing it tilted; release flat and level.

days.guide: Practice pancake and rim catches.

questions.q: When do you use a pancake catch?
questions.a: For a disc between chest and waist — clap hands together on it.

days.guide: Practice the forehand flick.

questions.q: What powers a forehand flick?
questions.a: A quick snap of the wrist.

days.guide: Pivot and pass to a moving receiver.

questions.q: Why throw ahead of a moving receiver?
questions.a: So the disc arrives where they will be, not where they were.

days.guide: Run the accuracy check.

questions.q: What is a key cue for the backhand?
questions.a: Step toward the target and keep the disc flat.

weeks.assessment_key: Accuracy check: 10 backhand throws to a target/partner 10 m away; record catches or target hits (6+ = proficient). Cue checklist: sideways stance, step toward target, flat release, follow through.

weeks.prep: Gather: flying disc, cones for end zones. Mark two end zones. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Running with the disc. The thrower must stop and pivot.
Arguing calls. Spirit of the Game means players resolve calls respectfully.

days.guide: Teach rules; practice the stall count.

questions.q: What is the stall count?
questions.a: The marker counts to 10; the thrower must release before 10 or it's a turnover.

days.guide: Practice cuts and give-and-go.

questions.q: What is a cut?
questions.a: A quick change of direction to get open.

days.guide: Play; resolve calls with Spirit of the Game.

questions.q: What is Spirit of the Game?
questions.a: Players referee themselves, follow rules and treat opponents with respect.

days.guide: Compare soccer and ultimate on a chart.

questions.q: Name one strategy shared by soccer and ultimate.
questions.a: Moving to open space to receive a pass.

days.guide: Give the quiz.

questions.q: What happens when a pass is dropped?
questions.a: Turnover — the other team gets the disc.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) a point is scored by catching the disc in the end zone 2) the thrower can't run with the disc 3) the marker counts the stall to 10 4) a dropped or intercepted disc is a turnover 5) Spirit of the Game = self-officiating with respect 6) shared strategies with soccer: moving to open space, passing, defending space. Sportsmanship self-assessment 1–4.

weeks.prep: Gather: basketball, cones, hoop if available. Pump up a basketball; set cones. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Slapping the ball with the palm. Dribble with fingertips.
Watching the ball. Eyes up.

days.guide: Ball-handling drills.

questions.q: Why use fingertips, not the palm?
questions.a: Fingertips give more control.

days.guide: Control vs. speed dribbles.

questions.q: How is a speed dribble different from a control dribble?
questions.a: Speed: ball pushed out ahead at waist height while running; control: lower, closer to the body.

days.guide: Crossover against a defender.

questions.q: When do you use a crossover?
questions.a: To change direction quickly and get past a defender.

days.guide: Peer checklist feedback.

questions.q: Give one dribbling cue.
questions.a: Eyes up; fingertips; keep the ball low; protect it with your body.

days.guide: Timed course.

questions.q: Why practice with both hands?
questions.a: So you can dribble away from defenders on either side.

weeks.assessment_key: Dribble course time (both hands) with checklist: fingertip control, ball at waist height or lower, eyes up, body protects the ball. Proficient = completes course without losing control using both hands.

weeks.prep: Gather: basketball, wall target, hoop. Make a wall target with tape. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Shooting with two hands pushing from the chest. Use one shooting hand with guide hand on side.
Jumping off the wrong foot on a layup. Right-hand layup: step right, jump off left.

days.guide: Chest, bounce and overhead passes.

questions.q: Where should a bounce pass hit the floor?
questions.a: About two-thirds of the way to the receiver.

days.guide: Form shooting with BEEF.

questions.q: What does BEEF stand for?
questions.a: Balance, Eyes, Elbow, Follow-through.

days.guide: Layups both sides.

questions.q: Footwork for a right-hand layup?
questions.a: Step right, then left, jump off the left foot and lift the right knee.

days.guide: Record and compare to BEEF.

questions.q: Your shots keep falling short. What might help?
questions.a: More leg power (bend knees) and a full follow-through.

days.guide: Shooting check.

questions.q: You made 12 of 30 shots. Percentage?

weeks.assessment_key: Shooting check: 10 shots from 3 spots (30 total); percentage = makes ÷ 30 × 100 (e.g., 12/30 = 40%). Form checklist (BEEF): Balance, Eyes on the rim, Elbow under the ball, Follow-through.

weeks.prep: Gather: basketball, hoop. Hoop or target. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Standing still after passing. Cut after the pass.
Crossing feet on defense. Slide.

days.guide: Practice give-and-go.

questions.q: What is a give-and-go?
questions.a: Pass to a teammate, cut toward the basket, and receive the ball back.

days.guide: Defensive slides.

questions.q: Where should a defender stay?
questions.a: Between their player and the basket.

days.guide: Box out and rebound.

questions.q: What does boxing out mean?
questions.a: Putting your body between your opponent and the basket to get the rebound.

days.guide: 2v2 games.

questions.q: Why spread out on offense?
questions.a: To create space for drives and passes.

days.guide: Diagram a play.

questions.q: Why does the give-and-go work?
questions.a: The defender watches the ball, letting the cutter get free.

weeks.assessment_key: Diagrammed play rubric: shows players, passes, cuts and explains why it works (e.g., give-and-go: pass, cut past defender, receive return pass near the basket). Observation: uses defensive slides, boxes out, moves after passing.

weeks.prep: Gather: basketball, hoop, whistle. Get a whistle; review referee signals. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Calling every bump a foul. Fouls are illegal contact that affects play.
Getting upset in pressure games.

days.guide: Learn violations and signals.

questions.q: What is a double dribble?
questions.a: Dribbling with both hands, or stopping and then starting to dribble again.

days.guide: 3v3 with student referee.

questions.q: What does a referee signal by rolling the arms?
questions.a: Traveling.

days.guide: Knockout and HORSE.

questions.q: How does pressure shooting help?
questions.a: Practices staying calm and keeping form.

days.guide: Mini-tournament with sportsmanship.

questions.q: Name a sportsmanship behavior.
questions.a: Shaking hands, helping opponents up, accepting calls.

days.guide: Quiz and redo the shooting check.

questions.q: How many points is a free throw?

weeks.assessment_key: Rules quiz: 1) traveling = moving the pivot foot or taking steps without dribbling 2) double dribble = dribbling with two hands or dribbling again after stopping 3) personal foul = illegal contact 4) free throws are worth 1 point; regular baskets 2; shots beyond the arc 3 5) the ball goes out of bounds to the team that didn't touch it last. Shooting improvement: compare percentage with Week 12.

weeks.prep: Gather: volleyball or beach ball, net or rope. Use a volleyball or beach ball; string a rope as a net. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Swinging the arms on a forearm pass. Keep a flat platform and use the legs.
Setting with palms. Use fingertips in a triangle shape.

days.guide: Teach ready position; self-toss passes.

questions.q: Describe the ready position.
questions.a: Feet shoulder-width, knees bent, weight forward, arms out in front.

days.guide: Partner bump; count passes.

questions.q: Where should the ball contact on a forearm pass?
questions.a: On the flat forearms above the wrists.

days.guide: Teach the overhead set.

questions.q: How do the hands form for a set?
questions.a: A triangle/window above the forehead, contacting with fingertips.

days.guide: Pass to set.

questions.q: What is the usual order of contacts?
questions.a: Pass (bump), set, then attack/hit.

days.guide: Passing check.

questions.q: Why use your legs on a pass?
questions.a: Legs provide power and control instead of swinging arms.

weeks.assessment_key: Passing check: 10 forearm passes from a toss to a target zone; record successes (6+ proficient). Cues: ready position, platform (hands together, thumbs parallel, arms straight), contact on forearms, lift with legs.

weeks.prep: Gather: volleyball, net or rope. Mark 6 m and 9 m serving lines. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Tossing too high on the underhand serve. Hold or drop the ball slightly.
Everyone chasing the ball. Call 'mine' and cover zones.

days.guide: Underhand serves at 6 then 9 m.

questions.q: Cues for an underhand serve?
questions.a: Opposite foot forward, hold ball at waist, swing arm back and forward, hit with heel of the hand, follow through to target.

days.guide: Overhand serve toss and contact.

questions.q: Where should the overhand toss go?
questions.a: Just in front of the hitting shoulder, about an arm's length high.

days.guide: Cooperative rally, 3 contacts per side.

questions.q: How many contacts is a team allowed?
questions.a: Three.

days.guide: Modified game with rotation.

questions.q: Which way do players rotate?
questions.a: Clockwise, when your team wins the serve.

days.guide: Write placement reflection.

questions.q: Where should you aim to win points?
questions.a: Open spaces, deep corners, or between two players.

weeks.assessment_key: Serve accuracy: successes out of 10 over the net and in bounds. Game observation: calls the ball, uses three contacts, rotates correctly, places the ball into open space or deep corners. Reflection: placing the ball where defenders are not (open spaces, deep corners, between players) wins points.

weeks.prep: Gather: badminton rackets and shuttlecocks, net or rope. Badminton set and rope net. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Gripping like a frying pan. Use a handshake grip.
Hitting every shot hard. Mix clears and drops.

days.guide: Handshake grip; short and long serves.

questions.q: Where must the shuttle be hit on a serve?
questions.a: Below the waist, underhand.

days.guide: Forehand and backhand rallies.

questions.q: How does a backhand grip change?
questions.a: The thumb presses flat on the back of the handle.

days.guide: Clears and drops.

questions.q: Why use a clear?
questions.a: To push the opponent to the back of the court and gain time.

days.guide: Singles with placement.

questions.q: What placement strategy wins points?
questions.a: Alternate deep clears and short drops to move your opponent.

days.guide: Rally and clear check.

questions.q: What is a drop shot?
questions.a: A soft shot that falls just over the net.

weeks.assessment_key: Check: longest rally count and clears out of 10 that land in the back third. Cues: handshake grip; serve underhand, contact below the waist; clear = high and deep; drop = soft, just over the net.

weeks.prep: Gather: volleyball, badminton set, fitness log. Fitness log with baseline scores ready. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Comparing scores with others. Compare with your own baseline.
Giving up on a goal not yet met. Adjust the plan.

days.guide: Play four square and paddle games.

questions.q: What is placement in net games?
questions.a: Sending the ball where the opponent can't easily return it.

days.guide: Retest PACER/mile and push-ups.

questions.q: Baseline 18 laps, now 25. Improvement?
questions.a: 7 laps.

days.guide: Tournament round 1.

questions.q: How do you show good sportsmanship after losing?
questions.a: Shake hands and congratulate the winner.

days.guide: Tournament finals.

questions.q: Give a positive comment to an opponent.
questions.a: 'Great serve!' 'Good game!'

days.guide: Update SMART goals.

questions.q: What if a goal was already met?
questions.a: Set a new, slightly higher goal.

weeks.assessment_key: Mid-year comparison: PACER/mile and push-ups vs. baseline with improvement calculated (e.g., 20 → 26 laps = +6). Updated SMART goals that reflect new data.

weeks.prep: Gather: softball glove or soft ball, tennis balls, bucket target. Use soft balls or tennis balls at first; set a bucket target. Check the space for hazards, have water ready, and start every session with the dynamic warm-up.
misconceptions: Throwing 'all arm' with feet square. Step with the opposite foot and rotate hips.
Catching fly balls at the chest. Reach up with two hands above the head.

days.guide: Practice overhand throws at a target.

questions.q: Which foot steps forward when a right-hander throws?
questions.a: The left foot (opposite foot).

days.guide: Field ground balls with alligator hands.

questions.q: What are 'alligator hands'?
questions.a: Glove open low to the ground with the throwing hand above it like a jaw to trap the ball.

days.guide: Catch fly balls; call 'mine'.

questions.q: Why call 'mine'?
questions.a: To avoid collisions and show who will catch it.

days.guide: Learn the crow hop; measure distance.

questions.q: What does a crow hop add?
questions.a: Momentum toward the target, for a longer, stronger throw.

days.guide: Accuracy check.

questions.q: Where should your throwing arm finish?
questions.a: Across the body toward the opposite hip.

weeks.assessment_key: Accuracy check: 10 throws at a target from 15 m; record hits (6+ proficient). Throw cues: side to target, step with opposite foot, hip rotation, arm long, follow through across the body.
