days.guide: Diagram a neuron; trace receptor → nerve → spinal cord → brain → muscle.

questions.q: Name three parts of a neuron.
questions.a: Dendrites, cell body, axon.

days.guide: Run the ruler drop 10 times per hand; average.

questions.q: Why might the dominant hand be faster?
questions.a: It's practiced more, so the nerve pathways are used more.

days.guide: Two-point test on fingertip, palm and forearm.

questions.q: Where can you feel two points closest together?
questions.a: Fingertips — they have the most touch receptors.

days.guide: Blindfolded jelly bean test with and without nose held.

questions.q: Predict the effect of holding your nose.
questions.a: Fewer correct identifications.

days.guide: The child writes the CER.

questions.q: What part of the nervous system processes signals?
questions.a: The brain.

weeks.assessment_key: Data: reaction averages each hand, two-point thresholds (fingertip smallest), jelly bean accuracy with and without nose held. CER rubric — 4: a claim that answers the question, specific data as evidence (numbers from the investigation), and reasoning that connects the evidence to the science idea; 3: claim and evidence correct but reasoning thin; 2: claim with vague evidence; 1: claim only or incorrect. Expected: 'Smell affects taste: I identified 9 of 10 flavors normally but only 3 of 10 holding my nose, because much of flavor comes from smell receptors in the nose.'

weeks.prep: Gather: tray of 20 objects, towel, optical illusion images. Gather 20 small objects and a towel; print optical illusions.
misconceptions: Thinking memory is a perfect recording. Memories are rebuilt and can change.
Thinking illusions mean eyes are broken. The brain interprets signals using shortcuts.

days.guide: Study 20 objects 1 minute; list; repeat with a strategy (grouping or story).

questions.q: Name a memory strategy.
questions.a: Chunking/grouping, making a story, repetition, mnemonics.

days.guide: Investigate three illusions.

questions.q: Why do optical illusions fool us?
questions.a: The brain uses assumptions to interpret signals from the eyes, and illusions exploit them.

days.guide: Read two sources; make an infographic.

questions.q: What helps form long-term memories?
questions.a: Repetition, attention, sleep and connecting to existing knowledge.

days.guide: Make a 4-system poster for catching a ball.

questions.q: Which systems work together to catch a ball?
questions.a: Nervous (eyes and brain), muscular, skeletal, circulatory/respiratory.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test.

questions.q: What carries signals from the eyes to the brain?
questions.a: The optic nerve.

weeks.assessment_key: Infographic rubric: two sources summarized accurately (memories form as connections between neurons strengthen; repetition, sleep and meaning help). Poster rubric: catching a ball involves nervous (eyes, brain), muscular, skeletal, circulatory and respiratory systems. Unit 8 test sample: bones/joints/muscle pairs; blood path; diaphragm; digestion path; kidneys; neuron parts; senses.

weeks.prep: Gather: pizza box, foil, black paper, plastic wrap, tape, newspaper. Get a pizza box, foil, black paper, plastic wrap.
misconceptions: Thinking more foil always helps. Foil reflects light in; black paper absorbs; insulation keeps heat in.
Skipping the decision matrix.

days.guide: Research solar ovens; define criteria and constraints.

questions.q: Why are solar ovens useful in some places?
questions.a: They cook without fuel, saving wood and reducing smoke.

days.guide: List how each science idea helps.

questions.q: Why line the bottom with black paper?
questions.a: Black absorbs light, converting it to thermal energy.

days.guide: Sketch three designs; use a matrix.

questions.q: Why does plastic wrap help?
questions.a: It traps warm air inside (greenhouse effect) and reduces convection losses.

days.guide: Build the prototype.

questions.q: Why angle the reflector flap?
questions.a: To reflect more sunlight into the box.

days.guide: Write the design brief; predict max temperature.

questions.q: What does newspaper insulation do?
questions.a: Slows heat loss by conduction.

weeks.assessment_key: Design brief rubric — 4: problem, criteria (reach 60°C), constraints, science justification (reflection, absorption, insulation, greenhouse effect), chosen design with matrix scores, prediction with reasoning; 3: one gap; 2: no science reasoning; 1: incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: solar oven, oven thermometer, s'mores ingredients. Use an oven thermometer; check the forecast for sun.
misconceptions: Changing several features at once.
Opening the lid often, letting heat out.

days.guide: Test in direct sun; record every 5 minutes.

questions.q: Why record every 5 minutes?
questions.a: To see the heating pattern over time, not just the final temperature.

days.guide: Graph and compare designs.

questions.q: What does a flat section on the graph mean?
questions.a: Energy coming in equals energy escaping.

days.guide: Make one modification and explain.

questions.q: Why change only one feature?
questions.a: So any change in performance can be attributed to it.

days.guide: Retest; try a s'more.

questions.q: How did the graph change?
questions.a: Answers vary; expect a faster rise or higher max if the change improved transfer.

days.guide: Write a paragraph about the modification.

questions.q: Which heat transfer did more insulation reduce?
questions.a: Conduction.

weeks.assessment_key: Analysis rubric — 4: two graphs compared, one change explained by heat transfer (e.g., extra insulation reduced conduction loss, raising maximum temperature from 52°C to 63°C); 3: comparison without explanation; 2: one test only; 1: incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather: science notebook, slides or poster. Gather the science notebook and photos for the presentation.
misconceptions: Presenting results without explaining the science.
Treating units as separate. Energy connects them.

days.guide: Build the presentation.

questions.q: What should a capstone presentation include?
questions.a: Problem, criteria/constraints, designs, data, modifications and conclusions.

days.guide: Present and answer questions.

questions.q: Explain how your oven converts sunlight to thermal energy.
questions.a: Light passes through the plastic, is absorbed by black surfaces and becomes thermal energy, which is trapped by the wrap and insulation.

days.guide: Make an energy concept map.

questions.q: How does energy connect weather and the water cycle?
questions.a: The sun's energy evaporates water and unevenly heats Earth, driving winds, currents and weather.

days.guide: Give the cumulative assessment.

questions.q: What do cells use energy from food for?
questions.a: To carry out life processes (mitochondria release the energy).

days.guide: The child writes a reflection.

questions.q: What makes a good scientific question for next year?
questions.a: A testable question with measurable variables.

weeks.assessment_key: Capstone rubric — 4: clear problem, design process, data graphs, science explanations, answers questions accurately; 3: minor gaps; 2: limited science; 1: incomplete. Cumulative assessment sample: independent/dependent variables; particle motion and temperature; conduction/convection/radiation; water cycle; fronts; global winds; rain shadow; greenhouse effect; earthquakes along faults; magnetic and electric forces; gravity; KE and PE; cell theory and organelles; body systems.
